lessons.title: Introduction to Biological Molecules and Bio-elements
lessons.notes_html:
Biological molecules and bio-elements

Six bio-elements make about 98% of the living system. These elements form carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

  • Carbon: one of the six bio-elements that make about 98% of the living system.
  • Hydrogen: one of the six bio-elements that make about 98% of the living system.
  • Oxygen: one of the six bio-elements that make about 98% of the living system.
  • Nitrogen: one of the six bio-elements that make about 98% of the living system.
  • Phosphorus: one of the six bio-elements that make about 98% of the living system.
  • Sulphur: one of the six bio-elements that make about 98% of the living system.

Other essential elements

The remaining elements are present in small amounts but are also essential.

  • Calcium
  • Potassium
  • Sodium
  • Chlorine
  • Magnesium
  • Iron

Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphurAbout 98% of the living system

Polymers and hydrolysis

A polymer of 21 monomers has 20 bonds between them, so 20 water molecules are needed to completely hydrolyse it and break all the bonds.

Chain: 21 monomers → 20 bonds between them → 20 water molecules needed for complete hydrolysis.

lessons.title: Water — Importance and Properties
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrogen bond between water molecules

The weak attraction between the partial positive hydrogen of one water molecule and the partial negative oxygen of another is a hydrogen bond. The slight negative charge at one end of one water molecule is attracted to the slight positive charge of another water molecule.

Hydrophobic exclusion

Non-polar oil molecules are excluded by water and come together, which is called hydrophobic exclusion. This is the tendency of water to coalesce oil drop into large droplet.

Why water is called amphoteric

Water is called amphoteric because it can behave both as an acid and as a base. Due to ionization, a water molecule can donate a hydrogen ion (H+) and act as an acid, or accept a hydrogen ion and act as a base.

This property helps water maintain pH and take part in many biochemical reactions in the cell.

  • As an acid: water donates a hydrogen ion (H+).
  • As a base: water accepts a hydrogen ion.
  • Role: helps maintain pH and takes part in many biochemical reactions in the cell.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates
lessons.notes_html:
How monosaccharides are classified

Monosaccharides are classified on the basis of the number of carbon atoms and the type of carbonyl group.

  • Trioses: 3C.
  • Tetroses: 4C.
  • Pentoses: 5C, like ribose.
  • Hexoses: 6C, like glucose.
  • Aldoses: having an aldehyde group.
  • Ketoses: having a ketone group.

Glycosidic bond

Two monosaccharides are joined by a glycosidic bond formed by condensation. The covalent bond between two monosaccharides is called a glycosidic bond.

Starch and cellulose

Both starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose; they differ in the type of glycosidic linkage. Cellulose is the main structural carbohydrate of plant cell walls and is the most abundant carbohydrate in nature.

Properties and roles of starch, glycogen, cellulose and chitin

  • Starch: the storage polysaccharide of plants, made of glucose units; it stores energy in seeds and tubers which can be broken down when needed.
  • Glycogen: the storage polysaccharide of animals, highly branched, stored in liver and muscles and quickly converted to glucose.
  • Cellulose: a structural polymer of glucose with beta linkages; it forms plant cell walls and gives strength and support, and humans cannot digest it.
  • Chitin: a structural polysaccharide containing nitrogen, found in fungal cell walls and the exoskeleton of arthropods, where it provides protection and support.

lessons.title: Proteins
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of proteins

Proteins are the most important organic compound of the cell which carry out virtually all of the cell's activities. Proteins work as enzymes, hormones, transporters and structural parts and carry out almost all cell activities.

Why amino acids are named so

Amino acids are named so because each molecule contains both an amino group (-NH2) and a carboxylic acid group (-COOH). These two groups are attached to the same central alpha carbon atom. The amino group gives basic character and the carboxyl group gives acidic character, so the name combines both groups.

Structure of an amino acid

An amino acid is an organic compound containing an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable R group attached to a central alpha carbon. About 20 different amino acids make all proteins.

Every amino acid has the same amino group, carboxyl group and alpha carbon; only the radical (R) group differs.

Peptide linkage formation

A peptide linkage is formed when the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of another amino acid. A molecule of water is removed in this condensation reaction, and the resulting -CO-NH- bond is the peptide bond. Repeating this process joins many amino acids into a polypeptide chain.

Chain: amino acid + amino acid → peptide bond (-CO-NH-) + water removed → polypeptide chain.

Classification of protein

Proteins are classified on the basis of structure into fibrous and globular proteins, and on the basis of composition into simple, conjugated and derived proteins. They are also classified by function.

  • Structural proteins: build body parts, e.g. collagen in connective tissue, keratin in hair and nails, and elastin in ligaments.
  • Functional proteins: perform specific jobs, e.g. enzymes catalyse reactions, haemoglobin transports oxygen, antibodies give protection and hormones like insulin regulate body activities.

lessons.title: Lipids
lessons.notes_html:
What are lipids

Lipids are a diverse group of organic compounds that are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents, and they include fats, oils, phospholipids and steroids.

Glycerol and acylglycerols

Glycerol is a three-carbon alcohol with three hydroxyl groups — a trihydroxy alcohol made of three carbon atoms — and forms the backbone of acylglycerols. Acylglycerols are formed by combining glycerol with one to three fatty acids; triglycerides store energy, provide insulation and protect organs.

Why fats provide more energy than carbohydrates

Fats provide more energy than carbohydrates because fat molecules contain a much higher proportion of carbon-hydrogen bonds and very little oxygen. On complete oxidation, one gram of fat gives about 9 kcal of energy, while one gram of carbohydrate gives about 4 kcal. Fats are also stored in a water-free form, so they store more energy in less space.

Saturated and unsaturated acylglycerols

Saturated acylglycerolsUnsaturated acylglycerols

Usually solid at room temperature, e.g. animal fatsUsually liquid at room temperature, e.g. plant oils

Waxes

Waxes are esters of long-chain fatty acids with long-chain alcohols. They form waterproof coatings on leaves, fruits, skin and feathers, reducing water loss and giving protection.

Terpenoids

Terpenoids are a large and important class of lipids made up of repeating isoprenoid units (C5H8). They are classified according to the number of these units, such as monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, diterpenes, triterpenes and tetraterpenes. Carotenoids, which are tetraterpenes, act as photosynthetic pigments and give colour to carrots and leaves. Other terpenoids include rubber, steroids precursors, essential oils and vitamins A, E and K, showing their wide biological importance.

lessons.title: Nucleic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
What is nucleic acid

Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides that store and transfer genetic information; DNA and RNA are the two types.

How many steps involve in nucleotide formation

Nucleotide formation involves joining of three components in steps. First a nitrogenous base is attached to a pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) to form a nucleoside. Then one or more phosphate groups are attached to the sugar to make a nucleotide.

Chain: base + sugar → nucleoside → + phosphate → nucleotide. Thus base + sugar + phosphate are combined step by step to complete a nucleotide.

Mononucleotide — ATP

ATP is a mononucleotide consisting of adenine base, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups; its high-energy phosphate bonds store and release energy for cell activities.

  • Base: adenine.
  • Sugar: ribose.
  • Phosphate: three phosphate groups.

Dinucleotide — NAD

NAD is a dinucleotide formed by joining two nucleotides, one containing adenine and the other nicotinamide, linked through their phosphate groups. NAD works as a coenzyme and carries hydrogen and electrons during respiration.

What are conjugated molecules

Conjugated molecules are formed when biomolecules of two different groups combine chemically and act as one unit.

Glycolipids

Glycolipids are conjugates of lipids and carbohydrates. They are found in brain white matter, myelin sheath and membranes.

  • Components: lipids + carbohydrates.
  • Found in: brain white matter, myelin sheath and membranes.

Glycoproteins

Glycoproteins are conjugates of carbohydrate and protein. They work as receptors, transport proteins and blood group antigens.

  • Components: carbohydrate + protein.
  • Roles: receptors, transport proteins and blood group antigens.

Lipoproteins

Lipoproteins are conjugates of lipids and proteins. They transport lipids in blood plasma.

  • Components: lipids + proteins.
  • Role: transport lipids in blood plasma.

Nucleoproteins

Nucleoproteins are conjugates of nucleic acid and basic protein. They form chromatin, chromosomes and ribosomes.

  • Components: nucleic acid + basic protein.
  • Form: chromatin, chromosomes and ribosomes.

lessons.title: Enzyme Structure
lessons.notes_html:
What is an Enzyme?

An enzyme is a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up a specific chemical reaction in living organisms without being used up itself. Enzymes work in small amounts and remain unchanged at the end of the reaction. They need an optimum temperature and pH for maximum activity, lower the activation energy of reactions, and their activity can be increased by activators or decreased by inhibitors.

Structure of an Enzyme

Most enzymes are globular proteins made of one or more polypeptide chains folded into a specific three-dimensional shape. A small region called the active site is where the substrate binds; it has a binding site and a catalytic site. The active site binds the substrate and takes part directly in the catalytic reaction, and it has a definite shape and chemical nature.

Simple and Conjugated Enzymes

  • Simple enzymes: Enzymes that are simple proteins.
  • Conjugated enzymes: Enzymes consisting of a protein part called apoenzyme and a non-protein cofactor.
  • Cofactor: The non-protein part; it may be a metal ion, a coenzyme or a tightly bound prosthetic group.
  • Holoenzyme: The complete active form of a conjugated enzyme.

Prosthetic Group

A prosthetic group is a non-protein part that is permanently and tightly attached to an enzyme and is essential for its activity. It may be an organic molecule or a metal ion. Unlike a coenzyme, it does not separate from the enzyme during the reaction. Haem group in some enzymes is a common example of a prosthetic group.

Why Enzymes are Specific

Enzymes are specific because each enzyme has an active site of a definite shape and chemical nature. Only a substrate with a complementary shape can fit into that active site and form an enzyme-substrate complex. Therefore one enzyme generally catalyses only one type of reaction.

lessons.title: Mechanism of Enzyme Action
lessons.notes_html:
Mechanism of Enzyme Action

In enzyme action, the substrate first binds to the active site of the enzyme to form an enzyme-substrate complex. Binding stresses the substrate bonds and lowers activation energy, converting the substrate into products. An enzyme-product complex is formed, the products are released, and the free enzyme is ready to be used again.

  • Step 1: Substrate binds to the active site.
  • Step 2: Enzyme-substrate complex is formed.
  • Step 3: Substrate is converted into products.
  • Step 4: Products are released and the enzyme is free for reuse.

Lock and Key Model

The lock and key model says the active site has a fixed shape complementary to the substrate.

Induced Fit Model

The induced fit model says the active site changes shape slightly on binding. In induced fit, the binding of the substrate changes the shape of the enzyme's active site so that it fits the substrate more closely.

How Enzymes Lower Activation Energy

Enzymes work by dramatically decreasing the activation energy needed for a reaction. An enzyme reduces activation energy by binding the substrate at its active site and holding it in the correct position and stressed form. This brings reacting groups close together and weakens the bonds that are to be broken. The substrate therefore reaches the transition state easily with less energy, so the reaction proceeds faster at body temperature.

Effect on Free Energy and Equilibrium

Enzymes speed up a reaction by lowering activation energy, but they do not change the free energy change of the reaction. An enzyme only speeds up reaching equilibrium; it cannot change the position of equilibrium. If an enzyme is added where substrate and product are in equilibrium, nothing changes and the reaction stays at equilibrium.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Enzyme Action
lessons.notes_html:
Effect of Temperature

Temperature strongly affects the rate of enzyme action. At low temperature enzyme molecules have little kinetic energy, so fewer collisions occur and the rate is slow. As temperature rises, collisions increase and the rate roughly doubles with every 10°C rise until the optimum temperature is reached. For most human enzymes the optimum is about 37°C. Beyond the optimum, heat denatures the enzyme by destroying its three-dimensional shape, and the rate falls sharply to zero.

Why Enzymes are Temperature Sensitive

Enzymes are proteins, so their activity depends strongly on temperature. At low temperature they work slowly, and activity increases up to an optimum temperature, about 37°C for human enzymes. Above the optimum, high temperature breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's shape and denatures it, so activity falls rapidly. Hot-spring bacteria have enzymes with a high optimum temperature.

Effect of Substrate Concentration

At low substrate concentration, increasing the substrate increases the rate because more active sites are occupied. As concentration rises, more enzyme-substrate complexes form and product formation speeds up. Gradually the active sites become occupied and the rate rises more slowly. When all active sites are saturated, the enzyme works at maximum rate (Vmax) and the rate stays constant. Further increase in substrate then has no effect.

Effect of Enzyme Concentration

Enzyme activity increases with enzyme concentration because more enzyme molecules provide more active sites for the substrate. When substrate is available in excess, every increase in enzyme molecules increases the number of enzyme-substrate complexes formed per unit time. As a result, more product is formed and the rate rises in direct proportion, until the substrate becomes limiting.

lessons.title: Enzyme Inhibition
lessons.notes_html:
Enzyme Inhibition

Enzyme inhibition is the decrease or stoppage of enzyme activity by a substance called an inhibitor.

Competitive Inhibition

In competitive inhibition the inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site. It can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration, because the inhibitor competes for the active site and adding more substrate can overcome the inhibition. Competitive inhibition depends on the active site acting as a specific template whose shape the inhibitor mimics to block the substrate.

Non-competitive Inhibition

In non-competitive inhibition the inhibitor binds at an allosteric site, away from the active site, and changes the enzyme shape, so it cannot be overcome by substrate. A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site and changes the shape of the enzyme, so the reactant can no longer be acted upon effectively.

Competitive InhibitionNon-competitive Inhibition
Inhibitor competes with substrate for the active siteInhibitor binds at another (allosteric) site
Can be overcome by increasing substrate concentrationCannot be overcome by substrate

Feedback Inhibition

Feedback inhibition occurs when the end product inhibits the first enzyme of its pathway. For example, in the pathway X → Y → Z → A, product A binds to the enzyme that converts X to Y at a position remote from its active site and decreases its activity; X is the substrate of the first enzyme and A is the allosteric (feedback) inhibitor.

Activators and Inhibitors

ActivatorInhibitor
Increases the activity of an enzyme, often by helping the substrate bind or by removing an inhibitorDecreases or stops enzyme activity
Speeds up reactionsSlows down reactions

Significance of Inhibition

Inhibition is significant because it regulates metabolism, is used in drug discovery and helps identify disease conditions.

lessons.title: Enzyme Classification
lessons.notes_html:
Classification of Enzymes

Enzymes are classified on the basis of the reaction they catalyse into six groups: oxido-reductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases.

  • Oxido-reductases: Carry out oxidation-reduction reactions.
  • Transferases: Transfer a group.
  • Hydrolases: Break bonds by adding water.
  • Lyases: Break bonds without hydrolysis.
  • Isomerases: Rearrange atoms within a molecule.
  • Ligases: Join molecules in condensation reactions.

Classification by Substrate

Enzymes are also classified by substrate, according to the substance they act on.

Enzyme TypeSubstrate
ProteasesProteins
LipasesFats
GlycosidasesCarbohydrates
NucleasesNucleic acids

This classification shows the specific nature of enzymes: each group is named for the type of reaction it catalyses or for the substrate on which it acts.

Summary of the Two Bases

On the basis of reaction, oxido-reductases carry out oxidation-reduction, transferases transfer a group, hydrolases break bonds by adding water, lyases break bonds without hydrolysis, isomerases rearrange atoms within a molecule, and ligases join molecules in condensation reactions. On the basis of substrate, proteases act on proteins, lipases act on fats, glycosidases act on carbohydrates and nucleases act on nucleic acids.

lessons.title: Cell Wall and Plasma Membrane
lessons.notes_html:
Why the Plant Cell Wall Is Rigid

The plant cell wall is rigid because it is mainly made of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a matrix of pectin and other polysaccharides. Cellulose chains are held together by hydrogen bonds, forming strong bundles that resist stretching. In many cells lignin is also deposited, which makes the wall even harder. This rigidity gives shape, strength and protection to the plant cell.

Structure and Composition of the Cell Wall

The plant cell wall lies outside the plasma membrane and is mainly composed of cellulose, pectin and other polysaccharides, with lignin in woody cells.

  • Primary wall: thin and flexible, formed first.
  • Secondary wall: thicker and more rigid, deposited later.
  • Middle lamella: made of pectin; it joins adjacent cells.

The wall gives shape, mechanical strength and protection to the cell, prevents it from bursting, and still allows water and solutes to pass through it.

Why the Plasma Membrane Is Differentially Permeable

The plasma membrane is differentially (selectively) permeable because its phospholipid bilayer allows only certain substances to pass. Small non-polar molecules pass easily, while ions and large polar molecules need specific transport proteins. This selective passage is due to the hydrophobic core of the bilayer and the presence of channel and carrier proteins. It helps the cell maintain its internal environment.

Chemical Composition of the Plasma Membrane

The plasma membrane is mainly composed of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it, along with cholesterol and small amounts of carbohydrates. This fluid mosaic structure makes the membrane flexible and selectively permeable.

Functions of the Plasma Membrane

  • Regulating entry and exit: it regulates the entry and exit of ions, nutrients and waste products through diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
  • Receiving signals: membrane receptors receive signals from the environment and from other cells.
  • Cell recognition: glycoproteins help in cell recognition.

In this way the plasma membrane controls the cell's interactions with its environment.

lessons.notes_html:
The Cytoplasm

The cytoplasm is shown in both the animal cell and the plant cell. In plant cells, a large central vacuole reduces the volume of the cytoplasm. When a lysosome ruptures, its enzymes are released into the cytoplasm and digest the cell's own components. In prokaryotic cells, the ribosomes are free in the cytoplasm.

Rough and Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum

The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of tube-like channels of lipoprotein extending from the plasma membrane to the nuclear membrane. Both types transport materials within the cell and provide a surface for biochemical reactions.

FeatureRough Endoplasmic ReticulumSmooth Endoplasmic Reticulum
SurfaceHas ribosomes attached to its surface, giving it a rough appearanceHas no ribosomes on its surface
FunctionsTakes part in protein synthesis, folding and transport of proteinsInvolved in lipid and steroid synthesis, detoxification and storage of calcium ions

Golgi Complex — Structure and Functions

The Golgi complex consists of flattened membrane-bound sacs called cisternae, stacked together, with small vesicles around them. It is especially prominent in glandular cells.

  • Processing: products of the endoplasmic reticulum reach the Golgi complex, where they are modified, sorted, stored and packed into vesicles.
  • Delivery: these vesicles then send the products to their destination inside or outside the cell.
  • Forming lysosomes: the Golgi complex also forms lysosomes.
  • Secretion: it secretes substances such as hormones, enzymes and mucus.

Lysosomes — Compartmentalisation of Enzymes

In animal cells, hydrolytic enzymes are packed in lysosomes to prevent general destruction of cellular components. Lysosomes pack hydrolytic enzymes in a membrane-bound sac so they digest only targeted material and do not destroy the whole cell.

In Tay-Sachs disease, a lysosomal enzyme is missing, so complex lipids cannot be broken down and accumulate in cells, which become clogged with very large and complex lipids.

Lysosomes — Structure

Lysosomes are small spherical sacs bounded by a single membrane and filled with hydrolytic enzymes. They are formed from the Golgi complex, and a newly formed lysosome before it starts its function is called a primary lysosome. Their enzymes work best at acidic pH inside the lysosome, which protects the rest of the cell.

Lysosomes — Functions

  • Digestion: lysosomes digest food particles, worn-out organelles and invading bacteria and viruses.
  • Autophagy: they also carry out autophagy.
  • Autolysis: when they rupture, they cause autolysis of the cell.

Why Lysosomes Are Called Suicidal Sacs

Lysosomes are called suicidal sacs because they contain powerful hydrolytic enzymes capable of digesting the whole cell. When a cell is damaged or old, the lysosomal membrane may rupture and release these enzymes into the cytoplasm. The enzymes then digest the cell's own components, causing autolysis. This self-destruction is useful for removing worn-out cells and organelles.

Vacuoles

Plant cells contain a large central vacuole that occupies most of the volume enclosed by the plasma membrane. The volume enclosed by the plasma membrane of plant cells is often much larger than the corresponding volume in animal cells, because plant cells contain a large vacuole that reduces the volume of the cytoplasm and makes plant cells much larger in volume. A large central vacuole is a plant cell feature.

Peroxisomes and Glyoxysomes

Peroxisomes are mainly concerned with the detoxification of alcohol and the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide.

lessons.title: Organelles II — Mitochondria, Chloroplasts, Ribosomes, Cytoskeleton and Nucleus
lessons.notes_html:
Mitochondria — Energy Transformers of the Cell

Mitochondria are one of the main energy transformers of cells. They transform energy from food into ATP, the usable energy form of the cell.

Why Mitochondria Are Called the Power House of the Cell

Mitochondria are called the power house of the cell because they produce most of the cell's ATP during aerobic respiration. Glucose and other fuels are oxidised in the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain located in mitochondria. The energy released is stored in ATP, which powers all cell activities. Without mitochondria the cell would not get enough usable energy.

Structure of Mitochondria

Mitochondria are rod-shaped organelles bounded by a double membrane.

  • Outer membrane: smooth.
  • Inner membrane: folded into cristae that increase its surface area. The cristae carry the electron transport chain and ATP synthase for oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Matrix: the space inside the inner membrane, which contains enzymes, circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.

Because of their own DNA and ribosomes, mitochondria have a semi-autonomous existence in the cell. In a diagram of a mitochondrion, the outer membrane, the inner membrane/cristae and the matrix are labelled.

How Mitochondria Are Similar to Bacteria

  • DNA and ribosomes: they have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes like bacteria, and they can make some of their own proteins.
  • Double membrane: they are surrounded by a double membrane.
  • Division: they divide by a process similar to binary fission.
  • Size: their size is also similar to that of bacteria.

This supports the idea that mitochondria evolved from ancient bacteria.

Mitochondria in Plant and Animal Cells

Mitochondria are present in both plant and animal cells. They are a structure common to plant and animal cells.

Chloroplasts — Energy Converting Organelle

The chloroplast is called an energy converting organelle because it converts light energy into chemical energy. During photosynthesis, chlorophyll absorbs sunlight and uses it to make ATP and NADPH2, which then fix carbon dioxide into glucose. In this way solar energy is changed into stored chemical energy of food. No other organelle performs this conversion in plants.

Organelles That Contain DNA

Besides the nucleus, only chloroplasts and mitochondria contain their own DNA; ribosomes do not.

Ribosomes and Protein Synthesis

Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis, so protein-producing cells are rich in ribosomes. Large numbers of ribosomes are present in cells that specialise in producing proteins.

Cytoskeleton — Types, Structure, Composition and Functions

The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres that gives the cell its three-dimensional shape. It constantly reorganises itself according to the needs of the cell, and it also helps in intracellular transport of organelles and vesicles.

TypeMade ofFunctions
MicrofilamentsActinHelp in cell movement and muscle contraction
Intermediate filaments—Provide mechanical strength
MicrotubulesTubulin proteinForm cilia, flagella, centrioles and the spindle during cell division

The Nucleus

The nucleus is present in both the animal cell and the plant cell. The nucleus contains DNA; besides the nucleus, only chloroplasts and mitochondria contain their own DNA. The endoplasmic reticulum extends from the plasma membrane to the nuclear membrane.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis — Light Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Photosystems and Pigments

Chlorophyll-a is almost identical to chlorophyll-b, but the small structural difference between them is enough to give them a different absorptive (absorption) spectrum. In a photosystem, chlorophyll is organized along with other molecules, and chlorophyll and other pigments form the light-gathering antenna complex that passes energy to the reaction centre.

Why the Antenna Complex Contains Other Pigments

The antenna complex contains other pigments along with chlorophyll so that a wider range of light wavelengths can be absorbed. Accessory pigments like carotenoids and chlorophyll-b absorb light of different colours which chlorophyll-a alone cannot absorb well. They pass the absorbed energy to the reaction centre. This makes photosynthesis more efficient, especially in varying light conditions. Photosystem I is located in the non-appressed (non-stacked) regions of the thylakoid membrane, along with ATP synthase and NADP reductase.

Photosynthesis as a Redox Process

Photosynthesis is called a redox process because it involves both oxidation and reduction. Water is oxidized, losing electrons and releasing oxygen. Carbon dioxide is reduced, gaining electrons and hydrogen, and is converted into glucose. Since oxidation and reduction occur together in the same process, photosynthesis is a redox process.

Cyclic and Non-Cyclic Photophosphorylation

FeatureNon-Cyclic PhotophosphorylationCyclic Photophosphorylation

Electron flowLinear flow of electrons from water to NADP+Electrons are passed back to Photosystem I through carriers
ProductsOxygen is released, and both ATP and NADPH2 are producedNo oxygen is evolved and no NADPH2 is made, only ATP is formed

Both processes use light energy to make ATP by chemiosmosis across the thylakoid membrane.

How Cyclic Photophosphorylation Helps

In cyclic photophosphorylation, electrons from Photosystem I return to it through electron carriers, and only ATP is produced. This extra ATP is needed because the Calvin cycle requires more ATP than NADPH2. Cyclic flow therefore balances the supply of ATP and NADPH2 for carbon fixation. It also protects the plant when NADP+ is not available.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis — Light-Independent Reactions and Alternative CO2 Fixation
lessons.notes_html:
The Calvin Cycle — Light-Independent Phase

The light independent phase, or Calvin cycle, takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast and does not directly need light. This phase depends on the products of the light phase but itself is light independent. The sequence is: CO2 + RuBP (5C) → PGA (3C) → glyceraldehyde phosphate → glucose and other carbohydrates, with regeneration of RuBP.

  • Carboxylation: CO2 is fixed by RuBP (5C) with the enzyme Rubisco to form PGA (3C). Carboxylation in the Calvin cycle is carried out by the enzyme Rubisco carboxylase, which fixes CO2 onto RuBP.
  • Reduction: PGA is reduced to glyceraldehyde phosphate using ATP and NADPH2 produced in the light reactions.
  • Regeneration: Some of this product is used to make glucose and other carbohydrates, while the rest regenerates RuBP so the cycle can continue.

Why the Calvin Cycle is Called the C3 Cycle

The Calvin cycle is also called the C3 cycle because the first stable product of carbon fixation in it is a three-carbon compound. Carbon dioxide is fixed by RuBP with the help of Rubisco to form phosphoglyceric acid (PGA), which contains three carbon atoms. Plants using only this cycle are called C3 plants. Most common plants, such as wheat and rice, are C3 plants.

Alternative CO2 Fixation — C4 Plants

Some plants avoid photorespiration by alternative CO2 fixation mechanisms. In C4 plants like sugarcane and maize, CO2 is first fixed in mesophyll cells by PEP into oxaloacetate (4C), which is converted to malate and transported to bundle sheath cells, where CO2 is released for the Calvin cycle. In members of the grass family, oxaloacetic acid is the first / intermediate carbon-fixing compound that passes CO2 to the Calvin cycle.

Alternative CO2 Fixation — CAM Plants

In CAM plants like cacti and pineapple, stomata open at night and CO2 is stored as organic acids in vacuoles, then released in the day for fixation. CAM plants close their stomata during the day to conserve water in hot and dry conditions. They open stomata at night, when evaporation is low, and fix CO2 into organic acids stored in vacuoles. During the day these acids release CO2 internally for the Calvin cycle while stomata remain closed. This greatly reduces transpiration and helps succulent plants survive in deserts. Both C4 and CAM mechanisms keep CO2 concentration high around Rubisco and conserve water or increase efficiency.

lessons.title: Cellular Respiration — Glycolysis and the Krebs Cycle
lessons.notes_html:
Cellular Respiration

Cellular respiration is the breakdown of glucose by redox reactions to synthesize ATP, releasing energy for the cell. Aerobic respiration occurs in the presence of oxygen and completely oxidizes glucose to CO2 and water, producing a large amount of ATP through glycolysis, Krebs cycle and electron transport chain.

Glycolysis — Breaking of Glucose in the Cytosol

The breaking of glucose in the cytosol is glycolysis, an anaerobic process common to almost all cells. Glycolysis does not require oxygen and takes place entirely in the cytosol. The sequence is: glucose (6C) → phosphorylated glucose → two molecules of pyruvate (3C).

  • Phosphorylation: One glucose molecule (6C) is first phosphorylated using ATP and then split into two molecules of pyruvate (3C).
  • Net gain: A net gain of 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and 2 NADH2 molecules is obtained.
  • Fate of pyruvate: The pyruvate formed then enters mitochondria for aerobic respiration or is fermented in anaerobic conditions.

Oxidation of one pyruvate gives one acetyl CoA with 2 carbon atoms, which are fed into the citric acid cycle.

The Tricarboxylic Acid (Krebs) Cycle

The tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix. The sequence is: Acetyl CoA (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C) → oxaloacetate, releasing 2 CO2. Acetyl CoA (2C) combines with oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C), the first tricarboxylic acid. Through a series of steps involving oxidative decarboxylation, citrate is converted back to oxaloacetate, releasing 2 CO2. Oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate in the Krebs cycle forms α-ketoglutarate, releasing CO2.

  • Per turn: 3 NADH2, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP (by substrate-level phosphorylation) are produced.
  • Per glucose: Since one glucose gives two turns, the yield is doubled, and the reduced coenzymes then feed the electron transport chain.
  • Substrate-level phosphorylation: One glucose gives two turns of the Krebs cycle, and each turn forms one ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, so two ATP are formed.

lessons.title: Cellular Respiration — Electron Transport Chain, Chemiosmosis and Fermentation
lessons.notes_html:
ATP — Common Energy Currency

ATP is called the common energy currency of living systems because it stores and supplies energy for almost all cellular activities. Energy from respiration and photosynthesis is trapped in ATP and later released by its hydrolysis to ADP wherever work is done. All organisms, from bacteria to humans, use this same molecule for energy transfer. Just like money, it is earned, stored for a short time and spent on needs.

Electron Transport Chain and the Role of Oxygen

Oxygen is consumed directly as the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain, forming water.

Chemiosmosis and Oxidative Phosphorylation

Chemiosmosis is the process in which ATP is synthesized using energy of a proton gradient across a membrane. The sequence is: NADH2 and FADH2 → electrons pass through carriers → H+ ions are pumped, creating a gradient → protons flow back through ATP synthase → ADP and phosphate join to form ATP. Protons flow back through ATP synthase, and this flow drives the joining of ADP and phosphate to form ATP. Oxidative phosphorylation is this ATP formation linked with the oxidation of reduced coenzymes, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor. It produces most of the ATP of aerobic respiration in mitochondria.

Aerobic Respiration and Fermentation

FeatureAerobic RespirationAnaerobic Respiration / Fermentation

BreakdownCompletely oxidizes glucose to CO2 and waterGlucose is only partially broken down
ATPProduces a large amount of ATPOnly 2 ATP per glucose

Anaerobic respiration types include alcoholic fermentation, producing ethanol and CO2 in yeast, and lactic acid fermentation, producing lactic acid in muscles and some bacteria, with only 2 ATP per glucose.

Why Oxidation of Pyruvate Gives More Energy than Lactic Acid Fermentation

Oxidation of pyruvate in aerobic respiration completely breaks it down to CO2 and water through the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain. This releases a large number of ATP molecules from one glucose molecule. In lactic acid fermentation, glucose is only partly broken down and lactic acid still contains much unused energy. Therefore aerobic oxidation of pyruvate provides far more energy than fermentation.

lessons.title: Photorespiration
lessons.notes_html:
Photorespiration and the Need to Avoid It

Some plants avoid photorespiration by alternative CO2 fixation mechanisms. Both mechanisms keep CO2 concentration high around Rubisco and conserve water or increase efficiency. These alternative mechanisms are found in C4 plants and in CAM plants, in contrast to plants that use only the Calvin cycle.

Rubisco and Carboxylation

Carboxylation in the Calvin cycle is carried out by the enzyme Rubisco carboxylase, which fixes CO2 onto RuBP. In the Calvin cycle, CO2 is fixed by RuBP (5C) with the enzyme Rubisco to form PGA (3C), a three-carbon compound. Plants using only this cycle are called C3 plants, and most common plants, such as wheat and rice, are C3 plants. Keeping CO2 concentration high around Rubisco is the shared effect of the alternative mechanisms described below.

C4 Plants — Spatial Separation

In C4 plants like sugarcane and maize, CO2 is first fixed in mesophyll cells by PEP into oxaloacetate (4C), which is converted to malate and transported to bundle sheath cells, where CO2 is released for the Calvin cycle. In members of the grass family, oxaloacetic acid is the first / intermediate carbon-fixing compound that passes CO2 to the Calvin cycle. In this way CO2 is delivered to the Calvin cycle in bundle sheath cells while its concentration is kept high around Rubisco.

CAM Plants — Temporal Separation

In CAM plants like cacti and pineapple, stomata open at night and CO2 is stored as organic acids in vacuoles, then released in the day for fixation. CAM plants close their stomata during the day to conserve water in hot and dry conditions. They open stomata at night, when evaporation is low, and fix CO2 into organic acids stored in vacuoles. During the day these acids release CO2 internally for the Calvin cycle while stomata remain closed. This adaptation greatly reduces transpiration and helps succulent plants survive in deserts, while also keeping CO2 available for fixation during the day.

lessons.title: Viruses — Discovery and Structure
lessons.notes_html:
Structure of a Virus

A virus particle consists of a Protein coat (capsid), Spike (attachment protein) and Nucleic acid (DNA or RNA). The nucleic acid is either DNA or RNA, protected inside the capsid.

Living and Non-living Status

Viruses show both living and non-living characters. Outside a host they are inert particles that can be crystallized, have no metabolism and do not respire or grow, which are non-living characters. Inside a living host cell they reproduce, mutate and evolve using the host machinery, which are living characters. Because of this dual nature, viruses are placed at the boundary between living and non-living and are called acellular particles.

Survival Without a Host

Outside a host, a virus survives as an inert particle called a virion, protected by its protein capsid and sometimes an envelope. It shows no metabolism and can remain inactive for long periods on surfaces, in air, water or soil, depending on temperature and humidity. Some viruses survive unfavourable conditions in dormant form inside host cells or seeds. When a suitable host is contacted, the virus becomes active again and starts its infection cycle.

Positive and Negative Sense Viruses

A positive sense virus has single-stranded RNA that can act directly as messenger RNA and be translated into proteins by the host ribosomes. A negative sense virus has RNA complementary to mRNA, so it must first be transcribed into a positive strand by viral RNA polymerase before proteins can be made. This classification is based on the nature of the viral genome. Influenza virus is a negative sense virus, while polio virus is positive sense.

Baltimore Classification

The Baltimore classification divides viruses into seven groups according to their genome and method of mRNA synthesis. This system is widely used for virus classification.

  • Group I: double-stranded DNA viruses
  • Group II: single-stranded DNA viruses
  • Group III: double-stranded RNA viruses
  • Group IV: positive sense single-stranded RNA viruses
  • Group V: negative sense single-stranded RNA viruses
  • Group VI: RNA retroviruses that use reverse transcriptase
  • Group VII: double-stranded DNA retroviruses

lessons.title: Parasitic Nature of Viruses
lessons.notes_html:
Obligate Parasitic Nature

Viruses have no machinery of their own, so they use the host cell's organelles, enzymes and energy for their reproduction and evolution. Viruses evolve by using the cellular organelles, cellular enzymes and cellular energy — all of them. Outside a host they remain inert, and inside a living host cell they reproduce, mutate and evolve using the host machinery.

How a Virus Takes Over the Host Cell

Viruses cause diseases by penetrating host cells, multiplying inside them and damaging tissues. The pathogenicity of a virus depends upon the effective penetration of its genome into the host cell, after which it takes over the cell machinery. Pathogenicity also depends on host immunity and environmental conditions, including the immunity of the host body and the overall environment inside the body.

Formation of New Virus Particles

In assembly, the smaller proteins are cut down and viral proteins are cut/processed and combined with the viral genome to form new complete virus particles. This is the process by which a new virus structure is formed inside the host cell using host resources.

Dependence on the Host

  • No own machinery: viruses use host organelles, enzymes and energy.
  • No metabolism outside host: as a virion, the virus shows no metabolism and does not respire or grow.
  • Activity only in host: reproduction, mutation and evolution occur only inside a living host cell.
  • Survival as virion: protected by capsid and sometimes an envelope, inactive on surfaces, in air, water or soil until a suitable host is contacted.

Because of this complete dependence, viruses are described as acellular particles at the boundary between living and non-living.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of Bacteriophage
lessons.notes_html:
How Bacteriophage Infects Bacteria

A bacteriophage first attaches to specific receptors on the bacterial surface by its tail fibres. Its tail sheath contracts and the viral DNA is injected into the bacterium through the cell wall, while the protein coat stays outside. The viral DNA then takes over the bacterial machinery to make new phage parts. Finally the cell bursts and releases new phages, or the viral DNA may stay integrated in a lysogenic cycle.

Lytic Life Cycle

Attachment → Penetration (injection of DNA) → Synthesis of phage components → Assembly of new phages → Release by lysis of the host cell.

In detail: the bacteriophage attaches to the bacterial surface with its tail fibres → the tail contracts and viral DNA is injected into the cell, leaving the coat outside → the phage DNA takes over host machinery, host DNA is broken down and new phage DNA and proteins are synthesized → these parts are assembled into complete phages, and the enzyme lysozyme weakens the cell wall → the bacterium bursts (lysis) and releases a large number of new phages to infect other cells. Lysozyme made by the phage dissolves the bacterial cell wall, so new bacteriophages escape from the host cell.

Lysogenic Life Cycle

Attachment → Penetration → Integration of phage DNA as prophage into the bacterial chromosome → Replication of prophage with the host DNA during cell division. Under induction, the prophage may leave the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle. Both cycles begin the same way but differ after penetration.

Lytic vs Lysogenic Cycle

FeatureLytic CycleLysogenic Cycle
Action of phage DNAImmediately takes control of the bacteriumIntegrates into bacterial chromosome as a prophage
New phagesMany new phages are produced at onceProphage is copied silently with host DNA for many generations
Fate of hostHost cell is lysed (burst) to release phages, so the host diesInitially harmless; host survives
Later courseDestructive at onceMay later switch to the lytic cycle under certain conditions

lessons.title: Life Cycle of HIV
lessons.notes_html:
Reverse Transcription in HIV

Reverse transcription is the formation of DNA from an RNA template, the reverse of normal transcription. HIV carries the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which converts its single-stranded RNA into double-stranded DNA inside the host cell. This viral DNA enters the nucleus and integrates into the human chromosome as provirus. It then directs the production of new HIV particles, mainly in helper T lymphocytes.

Life Cycle of HIV

HIV attaches to CD4 receptors of helper T lymphocytes → HIV enters the cell → Its RNA is converted into double-stranded DNA by reverse transcriptase → This DNA integrates into the host chromosome as provirus → The provirus may remain latent or become active, producing viral RNA and proteins using host machinery → New HIV particles are assembled at the cell membrane and released by budding, acquiring an envelope → Gradually the helper T cells are destroyed, the immune system weakens, and AIDS develops.

Symptoms of AIDS

AIDS is the final stage of HIV infection in which the immune system is badly damaged. Its symptoms include prolonged fever, night sweats, rapid weight loss, chronic diarrhoea and swollen lymph glands. The patient suffers repeated opportunistic infections such as pneumonia and tuberculosis, and skin lesions may appear. Because helper T cells are destroyed, even common infections become severe and life-threatening.

Prevention and Control of AIDS

  • Blood safety: avoid contact with infected blood and body fluids; blood must be screened before transfusion.
  • Sterile equipment: sterilized or disposable syringes should be used; avoid sharing of needles and razors.
  • Safe practices: safe sexual practices are essential.
  • Mother to baby: an infected mother can reduce transmission to her baby by proper medical treatment during pregnancy and delivery.

There is no complete cure, so prevention and awareness are the main methods of control.

lessons.title: Viral Diseases
lessons.notes_html:
Viral Diseases in Humans

Viruses cause diseases by penetrating host cells, multiplying inside them and damaging tissues. Human diseases like influenza, hepatitis, dengue, polio, measles and AIDS cause millions of deaths and huge medical expenses. Poliovirus damages motor neurons of the spinal cord and causes paralysis, the disease poliomyelitis. Dengue fever, encephalitis and yellow fever are caused by arbo-viruses, which are transmitted by arthropods such as mosquitoes. Aedes mosquito is the vector that transmits dengue virus (and also chikungunya virus) through blood.

Each virus has a specific vector, mode of transmission and symptoms.

Pathogenicity and Economic Losses

Pathogenicity depends on host immunity and environmental conditions. Epidemics reduce working capacity, close schools and industries, and burden hospitals, as seen during COVID-19 when production fell in most countries. Plant viruses such as cotton leaf curl virus have caused losses of billions of rupees to Pakistan's cotton economy. Thus viruses damage both human health and the national economy.

lessons.title: Prions and Viroids
lessons.notes_html:
Prions

Prions are infectious protein particles that cause pathogenicity in humans and animals, e.g. mad cow disease. They are proteins that cause diseases in humans and animals. Prions are infectious particles made only of protein, with no nucleic acid, and they mainly cause diseases of the nervous system in humans and animals. Prions were discovered by Stanley Prusiner.

Viroids

Viroids are subviral particles of single-stranded RNA with some double-stranded regions, smaller than viruses and without a protein coat. They are smaller than viruses having single stranded RNA with some double stranded regions. Viroids are infectious particles made only of small single-stranded RNA, with no protein coat, and they cause diseases only in plants. Viroids were discovered by Theodor Diener.

lessons.title: Taxonomy of Prokaryotes and Archaea
lessons.notes_html:
Three Domains of Classification

Living organisms are classified into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Bacteria are true prokaryotes with peptidoglycan in their cell walls and are found everywhere. Archaea are also prokaryotic, but their cell walls lack peptidoglycan, their membrane lipids are different, and many live in extreme environments like hot springs and salty lakes. Eukarya includes all eukaryotic organisms — protoctists, fungi, plants and animals — whose cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. The domains differ in cell structure, biochemistry and habitat.

FeatureBacteriaArchaeaEukarya
Cell typeProkaryoticProkaryoticEukaryotic, with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
Cell wallPeptidoglycan presentPeptidoglycan absent—
Membrane lipids—Different from bacteria—
Habitat / membersFound everywhereMany in extreme environments like hot springs and salty lakesProtoctists, fungi, plants and animals

Protobionts and Their Relationship with Prokaryotes

Protobionts were the first non-cellular structures formed from organic molecules on the early Earth, considered precursors of living cells. They could absorb substances, grow, and show simple metabolism and division, but they could not reproduce exactly like true cells. Over time, protobionts that developed a nucleic acid system and a membrane gave rise to the first true prokaryotic cells. Prokaryotes are therefore regarded as the evolved, fully cellular descendants of protobionts. This relationship explains the origin of the earliest bacteria-like organisms.

Archaea in Extreme Conditions — Extremophiles

Archaea living in extreme conditions are called extremophiles. These archaea survive where most other organisms cannot live.

  • Thermophiles: archaea living in very hot places, such as hot springs.
  • Thermoacidophiles: archaea tolerating both heat and acidity.
  • Halophiles: archaea living in highly salty environments like salt lakes.
  • Methanogens: archaea that live in oxygen-free places such as marshes and animal guts and produce methane gas.

lessons.title: Bacteria — Ecology and Diversity
lessons.notes_html:
Bacteria in Nature

Bacteria are true prokaryotes and are found everywhere. They live in soil, air and water, as decomposers of dead matter, as nitrogen-fixing organisms in soil and in root nodules, and normally on and inside the human body.

Bacteria as Recycling Agents in Nature

Bacteria are called recycling agents because decomposer bacteria break down dead bodies of plants and animals and organic waste into simple inorganic substances. These substances, such as CO2, water, ammonia and minerals, return to the soil, air and water and are used again by plants. Without bacteria, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would remain locked in it. Bacteria also play a key role in nitrogen, carbon and sulphur cycles, keeping nature's recycling continuous.

How Bacteria Increase Soil Fertility

Bacteria increase soil fertility mainly by fixing atmospheric nitrogen and decomposing organic matter.

  • Rhizobium: living in root nodules of leguminous plants, it converts nitrogen gas into ammonia compounds usable by plants.
  • Azotobacter: a free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium in soil.
  • Nostoc: a cyanobacterium that also fixes nitrogen in soil.
  • Decomposer bacteria: they convert dead remains into humus and release nitrates through nitrification.

As a result the soil becomes rich in plant nutrients and crop yield increases.

Normal Flora of Bacteria

Normal flora means the microorganisms, mainly bacteria, that normally live on the skin and mucous membranes and inside the intestine of a healthy person without causing disease. The human body contains about one hundred trillion such bacteria. They prevent colonization by harmful pathogens by competing for attachment sites and nutrients. They also stimulate antibody production and some synthesize vitamins K and B12 in the large intestine. Internal tissues like blood and muscles are normally free of these microbes.

lessons.title: Structure, Shape and Size of Bacteria
lessons.notes_html:
Structure of a Bacterium

A bacterium is a unicellular prokaryote surrounded by a cell membrane and a cell wall of peptidoglycan, sometimes with an outer capsule. Its cytoplasm contains a single circular DNA in the nucleoid region, plasmids, 70S ribosomes and storage granules, but no membrane-bound organelles. Many bacteria have flagella for movement, and pili or fimbriae for attachment and conjugation. Some form resistant endospores in unfavourable conditions.

The labelled diagram of a bacterial cell in the textbook shows: capsule, cell wall, membrane, nucleoid (DNA), plasmid, ribosome and flagellum.

  • Capsule: an outer covering present in some bacteria, outside the cell wall.
  • Cell wall: made of peptidoglycan.
  • Nucleoid: the region containing a single circular DNA.
  • Plasmids: present in the cytoplasm along with 70S ribosomes and storage granules.
  • Flagella: for movement.
  • Pili or fimbriae: for attachment and conjugation.
  • Endospores: resistant structures formed by some bacteria in unfavourable conditions.

Structure of Peptidoglycan

Peptidoglycan is a large polymer that forms the rigid framework of the bacterial cell wall. It consists of long chains of two alternating sugars, N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM). Short peptide chains are attached to NAM units and cross-link the sugar chains together, forming a strong mesh-like network. This structure gives the wall strength, maintains cell shape and protects the bacterium from bursting. The enzyme lysozyme and the antibiotic penicillin attack this layer.

Gram stainingRetain the crystal violet stain and appear purpleLose the violet stain and take the pink counter stain
Resistance to antibiotics—Generally more resistant, because of the outer membrane

lessons.title: Modes of Nutrition in Bacteria
lessons.notes_html:
Autotrophic Mode of Nutrition

Autotrophic bacteria make their own food from simple inorganic substances. They do not depend on other organisms for food.

  • Photoautotrophic bacteria: such as cyanobacteria and green and purple sulphur bacteria, they use sunlight as an energy source for photosynthesis.
  • Chemoautotrophic bacteria: they obtain energy by oxidizing inorganic substances like ammonia, nitrites, sulphur or iron, and use it to fix CO2.

These bacteria are important in nutrient cycles, e.g. nitrifying bacteria in soil.

Photosynthesis Mechanism in Bacteria

Bacterial photosynthesis uses light energy to make food, but most bacteria use bacteriochlorophyll instead of chlorophyll and do not release oxygen. The light energy is trapped to form ATP and reducing power, which fix CO2 into organic compounds.

  • Anoxygenic photosynthesis: in purple and green sulphur bacteria, hydrogen sulphide acts as the hydrogen donor, so sulphur is deposited instead of oxygen being evolved.
  • Cyanobacteria: an exception — they use chlorophyll-a and water as donor and release oxygen, like plants.

Bacterial Growth

Phases of Bacterial Growth

  • Lag phase: cells adjust to the medium and grow in size but do not divide much.
  • Log (exponential) phase: cells divide rapidly at a constant rate.
  • Stationary phase: nutrients decrease and waste increases, so birth and death rates become equal.
  • Decline (death) phase: cells die faster than they are produced.

Transformation and Transduction

Both are methods of horizontal gene transfer and genetic recombination in bacteria, along with conjugation.

lessons.title: Importance of Bacteria
lessons.notes_html:
Economic Importance of Bacteria

Bacteria are economically very important. On the whole, their beneficial uses in industry, agriculture and medicine are enormous. Some bacteria cause diseases, food spoilage and damage to crops, which is their harmful side.

  • Food and industry: bacteria are used in making curd, cheese, vinegar and alcohol, and in leather tanning and retting of fibres.
  • Medicine: bacteria are used in making antibiotics such as streptomycin.
  • Agriculture: nitrogen-fixing bacteria increase soil fertility.
  • Environment: bacteria are used in sewage treatment and biogas production.

Bacterial Diseases in Man

Important bacterial diseases of man include cholera, typhoid, tuberculosis, pneumonia and tetanus. Cleanliness, vaccination and early treatment control these diseases.

  • Cholera: causes severe watery diarrhoea and dehydration and spreads through contaminated water; it is treated by oral rehydration and antibiotics and prevented by clean water and hygiene.
  • Typhoid: causes prolonged fever and abdominal pain and is prevented by vaccination and safe food.
  • Tuberculosis: affects the lungs with chronic cough, fever and weight loss, and is treated with a full course of antibiotics.

Bacterial Diseases in Plants

Bacteria cause several plant diseases, such as citrus canker, bacterial blight of cotton and rice, and crown gall. Signs and symptoms include water-soaked spots, cankers, wilting, yellowing, rotting and abnormal growths on leaves, fruits and stems. Infected plants show reduced growth and yield. Treatment includes spraying bactericides and antibiotics and removing and burning infected plants. Prevention is by using disease-free seeds, crop rotation, resistant varieties and disinfection of tools, so the disease does not spread in the field.

lessons.notes_html:
How Cholera and Typhoid Spread

Cholera spreads through water and food contaminated with faeces of an infected person containing Vibrio cholerae, especially during floods and poor sanitation. Houseflies can also transfer the germs to food. Typhoid spreads in a similar faecal-oral way through contaminated water, milk and food, and healthy carriers of Salmonella typhi can spread it unknowingly. Both diseases become epidemics where drinking water is unsafe and sewage disposal is poor. Boiling water and hygienic food handling prevent their spread.

Chemical Methods to Control Bacteria

  • Disinfectants and antiseptics: such as phenol, halogens (chlorine and iodine), heavy metals, soaps and detergents, aldehydes, ethylene oxide and oxidizing agents.
  • Food preservatives: used as a chemical method of control.
  • Antibiotics: also used to control bacteria.

Physical Methods to Control Bacteria

Physical methods include boiling, dry-heat oven, incineration, autoclaving, pasteurization, refrigeration, freezing, high-pressure processing, desiccation, lyophilization, ionizing and non-ionizing radiation and membrane filtration.

  • Autoclaving: sterilization by autoclave at 121°C for 15-40 minutes at 15 psi destroys even bacterial spores.

The choice of method depends on the material to be treated.

lessons.title: Protoctists — The Evolutionary Relationships
lessons.notes_html:
All Protoctists Are Eukaryotes

All protoctists are eukaryotes with a true nucleus, though some are autotrophic and others are heterotrophic.

An Artificial Taxon

Protoctista is considered an artificial taxon because it is a polyphyletic group made of organisms that do not share a single common ancestor. It includes plant-like algae, animal-like protozoa and fungus-like slime molds, which are very different from each other. They are grouped together mainly because they do not fit into the plant, animal or fungus kingdoms. Biologists therefore regard this kingdom as an unnatural, convenience grouping.

A Link Between Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes

Protoctista are regarded as a link because they are the earliest eukaryotes and resemble the ancestors of modern plants, animals and fungi. They show characteristics connecting simple prokaryotic organization with the advanced eukaryotic kingdoms.

  • Plant-like protoctists: resemble early plants.
  • Protozoa: resemble early animals.
  • Slime molds: resemble early fungi.

The three main eukaryotic kingdoms probably arose from protoctist ancestors. Hence protoctists form an evolutionary bridge between prokaryotes and modern eukaryotes.

General Characteristics and Diversity

Protoctista are eukaryotic organisms that do not belong to the plant, animal or fungal kingdoms. They may be unicellular, colonial or simple multicellular, and show autotrophic, heterotrophic, parasitic or absorptive nutrition. They mostly live in water or moist habitats. Because of this diversity, the kingdom is considered polyphyletic.

  • Plant-like protoctists: the algae, such as Chlorella and Ulva.
  • Animal-like protoctists: the protozoa, such as Amoeba and Plasmodium.
  • Fungus-like protoctists: slime molds and water molds, like Phytophthora.

All members of green algae have the pigment combination chlorophylls a and b, the same pigment combination as land plants. The amoeboid feeding stage of a slime mold is the multinucleate mass called plasmodium. Trypanosoma and Leishmania are disease-causing protoctists (flagellate protozoa) that cause sleeping sickness and kala-azar.

Classes of Protozoa — Based on Locomotion

Protozoa are grouped mainly on the basis of their mode of locomotion, e.g. pseudopodia, flagella, cilia or non-motile, and each class is named after its organ of movement.

SporozoaNo locomotory organelles in the adult stage; mostly parasitesPlasmodium

Ulva — Sea Lettuce

Ulva is commonly called sea lettuce because of its green leaf-like thallus found in sea water. It has a flat, green, leaf-like thallus only two cells thick, attached to rocks by a holdfast. Its cells contain a cup-shaped chloroplast and it photosynthesizes like plants.

Isomorphic Alternation of Generations in Ulva

Ulva shows isomorphic alternation of generations, in which the sporophyte and gametophyte look alike — the two generations are morphologically identical in shape and size. The diploid sporophyte, the plant that reproduces asexually, produces haploid zoospores by meiosis, which grow into identical haploid gametophytes. The haploid gametophyte, the plant that reproduces sexually, produces gametes that fuse to form a zygote. The zygote grows into a new sporophyte, completing the cycle. The names are based on the type of reproductive cells each generation produces.

lessons.title: General Characteristics of Fungi
lessons.notes_html:
Mycology

The study of fungi is called mycology.

Unusual Nuclear Behaviour in Fungi

Fungi show unusual nuclear behaviour. Their nuclei are haploid for most of the life cycle, and the diploid phase is only the brief zygote stage. During mitosis the nuclear membrane does not break down and the spindle forms inside the nucleus, which is called nuclear (closed) mitosis. In many fungi, two haploid nuclei from different parents coexist in the same cell for a long time — the dikaryotic condition — before fusing. Meiosis follows karyogamy immediately during sexual reproduction.

Features That Let Fungi Survive Almost Everywhere

Fungi survive in all environments where life is possible because of several features.

  • Spores: they produce enormous numbers of lightweight spores that spread by air and resist unfavourable conditions, and can remain dormant as spores when conditions are harsh.
  • Hyphae: hyphae can grow rapidly over and into food sources and absorb nutrients after external digestion.
  • Modes of life: they can live as saprophytes, parasites or symbionts on a wide range of substrates.
  • Tolerance: they tolerate a wide range of temperature, pH and moisture.

lessons.title: Evolutionary Relations in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
What Are Plants?

Plants are multicellular photosynthetic eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls, chlorophyll a and b, and alternation of generations.

General Characteristics of Plants

  • Cell structure: Multicellular eukaryotes with cell walls of cellulose and chloroplasts containing chlorophylls a and b.
  • Nutrition: Mostly autotrophic; they prepare food by photosynthesis and store it as starch.
  • Life cycle: Shows alternation of a haploid gametophyte and a diploid sporophyte generation.
  • Movement and range: Most plants are fixed in one place and show limited movement, ranging from tiny mosses to giant trees.

Evolutionary Relation in Plants

Land plants arose from green algal ancestors. Bryophytes were the earliest land plants without vascular tissue, followed by vascular seedless plants like ferns. Gymnosperms then evolved naked seeds, and finally angiosperms evolved flowers, enclosed seeds and double fertilization, becoming the most successful group.

The rapid diversification of land (vascular) plants occurred in the Devonian period.

Alternation of Generations

The life cycle alternates between a haploid gametophyte and a diploid sporophyte. The sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis, which grow into the gametophyte. The gametophyte produces gametes, which fuse to form a diploid zygote that grows into a new sporophyte. This alternation is found in all land plants, though the dominant generation differs.

How Plants Coped on Land

On invading land from the sea, plants faced drying, temperature changes and lack of support. They developed a waxy cuticle and stomata to control water loss, and spores with sporopollenin walls — sporopollenin makes spore and pollen walls tough, flexible and resistant to biodegradation. Vascular tissues and lignin gave conduction and support, roots anchored them, and protected embryos and, later, seeds and pollen allowed reproduction without free water.

Heterogamy and Oogamy

Heterogamy is important because the production of two different types of gametes allows specialization. The small motile male gamete can travel to the female gamete, while the large female gamete stores food for the early embryo. This division of labour increases the chances of successful fertilization and survival of the offspring. Heterogamy reached its most successful form, oogamy — a large non-motile egg and small motile sperm — in land plants, the most successful kind of reproduction, and led to seed formation.

lessons.title: Non-Vascular Plants — Bryophytes
lessons.notes_html:
Bryophytes — The Non-Vascular Plants

Hepaticae (liverworts), Anthocerotae (hornworts) and Mosses are the classes of Bryophytes. Bryophytes were the earliest land plants without vascular tissue.

Why Bryophytes Are Called Non-Vascular Plants

Bryophytes are called non-vascular plants because they lack true vascular tissues, xylem and phloem, for conduction of water and food. They also lack true roots, stems and leaves, having instead rhizoids and simple leaf-like structures. Water moves in them slowly by diffusion from cell to cell. For this reason bryophytes remain small and live in moist places.

Life Cycle of Moss

In moss, the dominant free-living generation is the haploid gametophyte, which grows from a spore through a filamentous protonema. The mature gametophyte bears antheridia producing male gametes and archegonia producing eggs; fertilization needs water and forms a diploid zygote. The zygote grows into a sporophyte (foot, seta and capsule) that remains attached to and dependent on the gametophyte. The capsule produces haploid spores by meiosis, which are dispersed by wind and germinate to repeat the cycle.

lessons.title: Seedless Vascular Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Seedless Vascular Plants

Vascular seedless plants like ferns followed the bryophytes in plant evolution. In living vascular plants the sporophyte is the dominant, free-living generation.

Psilophyta (e.g. Psilotum) are the most primitive living vascular plants, lacking true roots and leaves.

The Fern Gametophyte

The free-living heart-shaped gametophyte of a fern is called the prothallus.

Why Vascular Plants Are More Successful Land Plants

Vascular plants are considered more successful land plants because their xylem and phloem conduct water, minerals and food efficiently over long distances. Lignified xylem also gives mechanical strength, allowing them to grow tall and compete for light. They have true roots, stems and leaves, a dominant sporophyte, and in seed plants, pollen and seeds that free reproduction from water. These adaptations let them inhabit diverse and dry habitats and dominate the land flora.

How Leaves Evolved

Leaves evolved in two main ways during plant evolution:

  • Microphylls: As in Lycophyta, developed as small outgrowths (enations) of the stem that later received a single vascular strand.
  • Megaphylls: Found in ferns and seed plants, evolved from flattened and webbed branching systems: side branches became flat, arranged in one plane, and the spaces between them filled with photosynthetic tissue. Megaphylls have a branched vein system and a large surface for photosynthesis.

This evolution greatly increased the photosynthetic efficiency of land plants.

lessons.title: Seed Plants — Gymnosperms and Angiosperms
lessons.notes_html:
How Seeds Evolved

Seeds evolved from the heterospory of earlier plants, in which two types of spores, microspores and megaspores, were produced. The megaspore was retained inside the megasporangium (ovule) on the parent plant instead of being shed. A protective integument developed around the ovule, and pollen delivered the male gamete without needing water. After fertilization the ovule became the seed, containing an embryo with stored food. This gave plants a great advantage for survival and dispersal on land.

Gymnosperms — Naked Seeds

Gymnosperms have naked seeds because their ovules and seeds are not enclosed in an ovary; they lie exposed on cone scales. The word gymnosperm itself means 'naked seed'. Gymnosperms evolved naked seeds before angiosperms evolved flowers and enclosed seeds.

Resins, turpentine and pine oil are obtained from pines (Pinus).

The Flower — Reproductive Part of the Plant

The flower is called the reproductive part of the plant because it bears the male and female reproductive organs. The stamen (anther and filament) produces pollen grains containing male gametes, and the carpel (stigma, style and ovary) contains ovules with the egg. Pollination and fertilization occur through the flower, after which the ovary forms fruit and ovules form seeds.

In banana, the inflorescence/flowers are covered by one or many large bracts called spathes.

Double Fertilization in Angiosperms

Double fertilization is the characteristic feature of angiosperms (flowering plants). Fertilization in angiosperms is called double fertilization because two fusions occur inside the embryo sac. One male gamete fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote (syngamy). The second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form a triploid primary endosperm nucleus, which develops into endosperm, the food tissue for the embryo. Since two fertilization events take place together, it is called double fertilization.

lessons.title: Characteristics of Animals and Criteria of Classification
lessons.notes_html:
Characteristics of Animals

Animals are multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes without cell walls. Among the terms listed, the (Hox) genes that control animal body patterning are properly associated only with animals; cell wall and autotrophy are absent in animals, and sexual reproduction also occurs in plants and fungi.

How Animals Are Classified

Animals are classified into about 33 phyla on the basis of their evolutionary relationships and body organization. Only nine major phyla, from Porifera to Chordata, are usually studied in depth, while the rest are minor phyla. Comparative morphology and embryology provide the main clues.

Basic Factors of Classification

  • Level of organization: cellular, tissue, organ or organ-system level.
  • Number of germ layers: diploblastic or triploblastic.
  • Symmetry: asymmetrical, radial or bilateral.
  • Coelom: animals may be acoelomate, pseudocoelomate or true coelomate.
  • Fate of the blastopore: divides triploblastic coelomates into protostomes and deuterostomes.
  • Notochord: presence of a notochord separates chordates from invertebrates.

An adult animal that possesses bilateral symmetry is also triploblastic, with three germ layers, though it may not be coelomate, protostome or deuterostome. Bilateria encompasses all the others, as coelomates, protostomes and triploblastic animals are all subgroups of bilaterally symmetrical animals.

Diploblastic and Triploblastic Animals

DiploblasticTriploblastic
Develop from only two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm, with a jelly-like mesoglea between them, such as cnidarians.Develop from three germ layers, ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. The mesoderm allows formation of complex organs, muscles and, in many, a coelom, so they show a much higher level of organization.

Protostomes and Deuterostomes

ProtostomesDeuterostomes
The blastopore, the first opening of the embryo, develops into the mouth; the word protostome means 'mouth first' and the anus is formed later at a separate place. They generally show spiral and determinate cleavage, and the mouth develops from or near the blastopore. Molluscs, annelids and arthropods belong to this group.The blastopore becomes the anus and the mouth is formed secondarily.

Phylum Porifera — Sponges

Sponges are considered the simplest animals, in phylum Porifera. They are placed in the animal kingdom because they are multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes without cell walls, like other animals. They ingest food particles, have animal-like cells such as choanocytes, and reproduce sexually producing a free-swimming larva. Although they have only a cellular level of organization and lack true tissues, their nutrition, structure and development clearly show animal affinities.

  • Sponges: associated with spicules, their structural material.
  • Spicule formation: amoebocytes (scleroblasts) manufacture the spicules that form the skeleton / structural material of sponges.
  • Water movement: water enters the sponge through ostia, passes into the spongocoel and leaves through the osculum, i.e. Ostia → Spongocoel → Osculum.

Phylum Cnidaria

Cnidaria are associated with nematocysts. Cnidarians are diploblastic animals, developing from only two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm, with a jelly-like mesoglea between them.

  • Cnidaria: nematocysts.
  • Germ layers: two — ectoderm and endoderm.
  • Mesoglea: jelly-like layer between the two germ layers in diploblastic animals.

Flatworms (phylum Platyhelminthes) are named so because their bodies are dorsoventrally flattened like a ribbon or leaf. This flat shape keeps every cell close to the surface, so gases and food can diffuse easily, as they have no circulatory system. They are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and acoelomate animals.

  • Body form: dorsoventrally flattened like a ribbon or leaf.
  • Organisation: triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and acoelomate.

lessons.notes_html:
Phylum Annelida — Segmented Worms

Segmented worms (annelids) move by setae / parapodia, not pseudopodia; pseudopodia belong to Amoeba, so the pair segmented worm → pseudopodia is incorrect.

Evolutionary Adaptations of Annelida

  • Metameric segmentation: the body is metamerically segmented, with repeating units that allow specialization of different body regions.
  • True coelom: acts as a hydrostatic skeleton and permits efficient burrowing movement.
  • Circulatory system: closed circulatory system.
  • Digestive tract: complete digestive tract.
  • Nervous and excretory systems: well-developed nervous and excretory systems, with nephridia in each segment.
  • Locomotion: setae and, in polychaetes, parapodia help in locomotion.

These advances make annelids successful in marine, freshwater and moist land habitats, and show important evolutionary advances over simpler worms. Annelids belong to the protostomes.

Phylum Mollusca

Molluscs are soft-bodied, unsegmented, triploblastic coelomate animals, usually protected by a shell of calcium carbonate secreted by the mantle. Molluscs also belong to the protostomes.

  • Head: part of the body division.
  • Muscular ventral foot: used for locomotion.
  • Visceral mass: containing the organs.
  • Radula: a unique rasping feeding organ in the mouth in most molluscs.
  • Respiration: by gills or mantle cavity.
  • Circulatory system: mostly open circulatory system.
  • Examples: snails, mussels, octopus and squid.

lessons.notes_html:
Phylum Arthropoda

Arthropods are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical, coelomate animals with a segmented body divided into head, thorax and abdomen (or cephalothorax and abdomen). They belong to the protostomes.

  • Jointed appendages: arthropods have jointed legs / appendages, from which the phylum gets its name.
  • Exoskeleton: a hard exoskeleton of chitin that is moulted during growth.
  • Digestive system: complete digestive system.
  • Circulatory system: open circulatory system.
  • Respiration: by gills, tracheae or book lungs.
  • Size of phylum: the largest phylum, including insects, spiders, crustaceans and myriapods, adapted to every habitat.

Phylum Echinodermata

Star fish, brittle star and sea urchin are echinoderms.

Why Echinoderms Are Placed in Bilateria

Echinoderms are placed in Bilateria because their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical, showing their true evolutionary relationship. The radial symmetry of adults is a secondary adaptation to their slow-moving or sessile bottom-dwelling life. Their development is deuterostome-like, similar to chordates, which also supports this placement. Adult radial symmetry therefore does not reflect their ancestry.

  • Adults: radially symmetrical as a secondary adaptation.
