lessons.title: Mineral Nutrition in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
Where Plants Get Their Nutrients

Plants primarily obtain their essential mineral nutrients from the soil through their roots. Mineral nutrients are necessary because plants use them to build essential compounds and to carry out metabolism. Although needed in different amounts, each essential element has a specific role that no other element can fully replace. Without these minerals, plants show deficiency symptoms, poor growth and low yield.

Work Done by Some Nutrients

  • Nitrogen: needed for proteins and chlorophyll, and also for amino acids and nucleic acids.
  • Phosphorus: needed for ATP, nucleic acids and membranes.
  • Potassium: needed for enzyme activation and stomatal working.

Macro and Micro Nutrients

Essential inorganic nutrients are divided into macronutrients, needed in large amounts, and micronutrients, needed in trace amounts. Iron is a micronutrient, needed in trace amounts, while potassium, phosphorus and sulphur are macronutrients.

Macronutrients (large amounts)Micronutrients (trace amounts)
Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulphur, calcium, magnesium (and sodium, chlorine in the book's list)Iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper, molybdenum and cobalt

General Functions of Inorganic Nutrients

In general, inorganic nutrients form structural parts of proteins, chlorophyll, nucleic acids and membranes. They also act as enzyme activators and cofactors, maintain osmotic balance and pH, and take part in energy transfer, e.g. phosphorus in ATP. Deficiency of any essential nutrient disturbs growth.

Why Nitrogen Is Counted Among Mineral Nutrients

Nitrogen is included among mineral nutrients although it is not itself a mineral obtained as a metal, because plants absorb it from the soil in mineral (inorganic) forms, as nitrates and ammonium ions. It is an essential macronutrient required in large amounts for amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll. Atmospheric N2 cannot be used directly by most plants and must first be fixed into these mineral forms. For this reason nitrogen is listed with the mineral nutrients.

A Deficiency Sign to Remember

Deficiency of phosphate causes leaves to turn dull or bluish green (often with purplish tint) and growth is stunted.

Plants That Catch Insects

Carnivorous plants typically live in nitrogen-deficient soils. They grow in soils that are deficient in nitrogen and other minerals, so they cannot get enough nitrogen from their roots.

Why They Use Insects as Food

Carnivorous plants trap and digest insects to obtain nitrogen and other nutrients from insect proteins. Insects only supplement their mineral nutrition. They still make their own food by photosynthesis; insects are used because the soil cannot supply enough nitrogen through the roots.

  • Trap leaves: their leaves are modified into traps.
  • Forms of trap: the traps are like pitchers and snap traps.
  • Digestion: the traps work with digestive enzymes, and the plant digests the trapped insects.
  • Nutrients gained: nitrogen and other nutrients are obtained from insect proteins.

In short, carnivorous plants live in mineral-deficient soil, especially nitrogen-deficient soil, and meet the shortage by digesting insects, while photosynthesis continues as their way of making food.

lessons.title: Transport in Plants — Ascent of Sap and Translocation of Sugars
lessons.notes_html:
Two Transport Systems

Water moves up through the xylem in the ascent of sap, and sugars move through the phloem from a source to a sink. Active transport of sucrose into sieve elements at the source is called phloem loading.

Cohesion-Tension Theory — Ascent of Sap in Xylem

The cohesion-tension theory explains the ascent of sap in xylem. Transpiration from leaves creates a tension (negative pressure) at the top, which is the source of the pulling force. Water molecules cohere to each other by hydrogen bonds, forming a continuous unbroken column in the xylem, and also adhere to xylem walls. The transpiration pull is transmitted down this cohesive column, drawing water from roots to the tallest leaves. Thus cohesion keeps the column intact while tension pulls it upward.

  • Cohesion: supplied by hydrogen bonds between water molecules; it keeps the column intact.
  • Tension: its source is transpiration from leaves; it pulls the column upward.

Pressure Flow Theory — Movement of Sugar

According to the pressure flow theory, sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source (leaf), lowering their water potential. Water enters by osmosis from the xylem, creating high turgor pressure that pushes the sap towards the sink (root, fruit or growing part). At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and used or stored, water leaves the sieve tubes, and pressure falls. This pressure difference between source and sink drives the mass flow of sugars through the phloem.

Water entryWater enters by osmosis from the xylem; high turgor pressure is created
Mass flowSap is pushed towards the sink
UnloadingSucrose is unloaded and used or stored; water leaves and pressure falls

lessons.title: Gaseous Exchange in Plants and Osmotic Adjustment
lessons.notes_html:
Exchange of Gases in Plants

Gaseous exchange in plants occurs mainly through stomata in leaves and lenticels in woody stems, and through the general surface of roots. During the day, CO2 enters through open stomata for photosynthesis and oxygen produced is released. For respiration, oxygen diffuses in and CO2 diffuses out, day and night, according to concentration gradients. Guard cells regulate stomatal opening to balance CO2 uptake with water loss by transpiration. Intercellular spaces inside the leaf connect the stomata to all photosynthetic cells, making exchange efficient.

Water Potential and Osmotic Adjustment

Water potential describes the capacity/tendency of a living system to lose (or gain) water. In osmotic adjustment, plant cells accumulate solutes such as salts, sugars and amino acids in their vacuoles and cytoplasm. This lowers the cell's osmotic (water) potential, so the plant can draw and retain water even when soil water is scarce or salty. It helps maintain turgor, keeps stomata functioning and allows growth to continue during drought. Plants showing good osmotic adjustment are therefore more tolerant of water stress and salinity.

HalophytesPlants growing in salt marshes close to the sea; accumulate salts in vacuoles and may excrete excess salt, maintaining water uptake from saline soil

Why Desert Plants Reduce Leaf Size

Desert plants reduce their leaf size to decrease the surface area available for transpiration, so that water loss is minimized in hot and dry conditions. Small leaves, or leaves changed into spines as in cactus, also reduce heating of the plant. Photosynthesis is then often carried out by the green stem. This adaptation, together with thick cuticle and sunken stomata, helps desert plants conserve water.

lessons.notes_html:
What Growth Regulators Are

Growth regulators (plant hormones) are organic substances produced in very small amounts that control growth and development. Together these five regulators coordinate the plant's life activities.

The Principal Natural Auxin

IAA (indole acetic acid) is the principal natural auxin of higher plants, synthesized at the apices of stem and root. The production of lateral appendages (leaves and branches) depends on the activity of the apical meristem.

The Five Growth Regulators

RegulatorFunctions

CytokininsPromote cell division and delay leaf ageing, working with auxins in tissue growth

How the Five Work Together

  • Auxins: cell elongation, root initiation and apical dominance.
  • Gibberellins: stem elongation, seed germination and flowering.
  • Cytokinins: cell division, delayed leaf ageing, and tissue growth with auxins.
  • Abscisic acid: growth inhibition, dormancy, and stomatal closing during water stress.
  • Ethene: fruit ripening, leaf fall and senescence.

Some regulators mainly promote growth processes such as elongation, division and germination, while abscisic acid inhibits growth and promotes dormancy, and ethene promotes ripening, leaf fall and senescence.

lessons.title: Photoperiodism, Vernalization and Annual Rings
lessons.notes_html:
Photoperiodism and the Phytochrome Pigment

Phytochrome is the light-sensitive pigment that enables plants to measure day and night length, which is the basis of photoperiodism. It exists in two interconvertible forms, Pr and Pfr, which change with red and far-red light. The amount of active Pfr at the end of the night informs the plant whether the critical night length has passed. Accordingly, short-day and long-day plants initiate flowering at the proper season.

Vernalization — Flowering Promoted by Cold

Promotion of flowering by cold treatment is called vernalization.

Why Cold Treatment Is Needed for Germination in Some Plants

In some plants, seeds remain dormant even when water and oxygen are available, because growth inhibitors are present or the embryo is not fully ready. Exposure to a period of low temperature (cold treatment/stratification) breaks this dormancy by changing the balance of hormones, decreasing abscisic acid and increasing gibberellins. This ensures that seeds germinate in spring, not in the unfavourable winter. Hence cold treatment is necessary for germination of such seeds.

How Annual Rings Are Formed

Annual rings are formed by the seasonal activity of the vascular cambium during secondary growth. In spring, cambium produces large, thin-walled xylem cells (early wood), while in late summer and autumn it produces smaller, thick-walled cells (late wood). The sharp contrast between late wood of one year and early wood of the next appears as a ring. Counting these rings gives the approximate age of the tree.

WoodSeason FormedCells

lessons.title: Stages of Holozoic Nutrition and Types of Feeders
lessons.notes_html:
Stages of Holozoic Nutrition

Holozoic nutrition consists of five stages that occur in sequence in animals like man. Removal of undigested food is egestion, a separate elimination step; nutrition proper consists of ingestion, digestion, absorption and assimilation together with egestion as the final stage.

  • Ingestion: the taking in of food through the mouth.
  • Digestion: the mechanical and chemical breakdown of complex food into simple soluble molecules.
  • Absorption: the uptake of these molecules through the intestinal lining into blood.
  • Assimilation: the use of absorbed food for energy, growth and repair.
  • Egestion: the removal of undigested food from the body.

Enzymes play the most important role in digestion, as they chemically break down complex food into simple soluble molecules during digestion.

Teeth and Taking in Food

The thecodont condition means teeth embedded in sockets in the jaw bone, as in mammals and crocodiles. A child has 20 milk (deciduous) teeth, which are later replaced by permanent teeth. Incisors are sharp, chisel-shaped teeth meant for cutting and biting food. The pharynx is a common passage for food and air, so the part of the gut also associated with the respiratory system is the pharynx.

Types of Feeders — By Size of Food

On the basis of the size of food they take, animals are categorized into three groups. This grouping reflects different methods of ingestion in holozoic animals.

  • Microphagous: animals feed on tiny particles, e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium and many filter-feeding invertebrates.
  • Macrophagous: animals take in large pieces of food or whole organisms, e.g. Hydra, frog and man.
  • Liquid feeders: animals suck fluids, e.g. mosquitoes and leeches suck blood, butterflies suck nectar and spiders suck liquefied prey.

lessons.notes_html:
Digestion in Amoeba

Amoeba shows intracellular digestion. When Amoeba contacts a food particle, it extends pseudopodia around it and engulfs it by phagocytosis, forming a food vacuole. Lysosomes fuse with the vacuole and pour digestive enzymes into it, first making it acidic and then alkaline. The food is digested inside the vacuole and the soluble products are absorbed into the surrounding cytoplasm and assimilated. The undigested residue is removed by egestion when the vacuole reaches the cell surface and opens out.

Intracellular and Extracellular Digestion

Planaria shows both extracellular digestion in the gut cavity and intracellular digestion inside food vacuoles of gut cells.

SiteInside food vacuoles of cellsIn the gut cavity
ExampleAmoeba; also inside gut cells of PlanariaGut cavity of Planaria and higher animals

Sac-like Gut

A sac-like gut is an incomplete digestive system with only one opening that serves as both mouth and anus. Food enters through the mouth into a sac-like gastrovascular cavity, where extracellular and intracellular digestion take place. Undigested residue is egested through the same opening, so feeding and egestion cannot occur at the same time. Hydra and Planaria are suitable examples of animals with a sac-like gut. It is simpler than the tube-like gut of higher animals, which has separate mouth and anus.

lessons.notes_html:
Digestion in the Stomach

In the stomach, food is churned by muscular contractions and mixed with gastric juice to form a semi-liquid chyme. Rugae are the folds of the inner wall of the stomach that allow it to expand and help in churning food. Stomach digestion is mainly of proteins.

Gastric juice contains HCl, which kills germs, provides an acidic medium and converts inactive pepsinogen into pepsin. Pepsin begins protein digestion, breaking proteins into peptones, while in infants rennin curdles milk protein. Partly digested food is gradually released into the duodenum through the pyloric sphincter.

How the Stomach is Protected Against Strong HCl

The stomach is protected from its own strong HCl and pepsin by a thick layer of mucus secreted by its inner wall, which forms a physical barrier. The epithelial cells of the stomach lining are tightly joined and are replaced rapidly when damaged. Pepsin is secreted in an inactive form, pepsinogen, and is activated only in the lumen. Bicarbonate in the mucus also neutralizes acid near the wall. Together these protections prevent autodigestion of the stomach.

  • Mucus barrier: thick mucus layer secreted by the inner wall forms a physical barrier.
  • Tight epithelial lining: epithelial cells are tightly joined and replaced rapidly when damaged.
  • Inactive enzyme: pepsin secreted as pepsinogen, activated only in the lumen.
  • Bicarbonate: bicarbonate in the mucus neutralizes acid near the wall.

lessons.notes_html:
Digestion in the Small Intestine

In the small intestine, chyme is mixed with bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice in the duodenum and jejunum, and digestion of all food types is completed here. Pancreatic amylase, lipase and proteases and intestinal enzymes convert carbohydrates to glucose, fats to fatty acids and glycerol, and proteins to amino acids.

Absorption in the Small Intestine

The products are absorbed through the villi: glucose, amino acids, vitamins and salts enter blood capillaries, while fatty acids and glycerol enter the lacteal (lymph) of the villus. The enormous surface provided by folds, villi and microvilli makes absorption highly efficient.

How the Internal Surface Area is Increased

The internal surface area of the small intestine is greatly increased in three ways. These structures multiply the absorptive area many times. A large surface area, thin walls and a rich blood and lymph supply make absorption of digested food very efficient.

  • Circular folds: the inner wall has circular folds.
  • Villi: the surface bears millions of finger-like villi.
  • Microvilli: each epithelial cell of a villus has tiny microvilli forming a brush border.

lessons.title: Accessory Glands and the Large Intestine
lessons.notes_html:
Accessory Glands of the Gut

The accessory glands of the human gut are the salivary glands, liver and pancreas, along with glands in the stomach and intestinal walls. Together these glands make complete chemical digestion possible.

  • Salivary glands: secrete saliva containing amylase that starts starch digestion and moistens food. There are six salivary glands, i.e. three pairs (parotid, submaxillary/submandibular and sublingual), opening into the oral cavity.
  • Liver: produces bile, which emulsifies fats, and also processes absorbed nutrients carried by the hepatic portal vein.
  • Pancreas: secretes pancreatic juice with enzymes for proteins, fats and carbohydrates and also insulin.
  • Gastric and intestinal glands: add their own juices.

How Bile Helps in Digestion of Fats

Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder, contains bile salts but no enzymes. Bile salts break large fat globules into tiny droplets, a process called emulsification, which greatly increases the surface area of fats. This allows the enzyme lipase to digest fats quickly into fatty acids and glycerol. Bile also neutralizes the acidic chyme from the stomach, providing the alkaline medium needed by intestinal enzymes.

Role of the Large Intestine

The large intestine mainly absorbs water and salts from the liquid material received from the small intestine, converting it into semi-solid faeces. It also absorbs some vitamins produced by its bacteria, such as vitamin K and B vitamins. Its mucus lubricates the passage of faeces. Finally, it stores faeces temporarily and removes them by egestion through the anus. It has no role in enzymatic digestion of food.

Bacteria in the Large Intestine

Bacteria reach the large intestine with food and water and find there a warm environment, moisture and a continuous supply of undigested material on which to feed. Unlike the stomach, the large intestine has no strong acid to kill them, so they multiply and live as a normal flora. These bacteria are mostly harmless or useful; they produce vitamins and gases and help form faeces. Their presence is therefore a normal feature of the gut.

lessons.title: Eating Disorders — Obesity and Anorexia Nervosa
lessons.notes_html:
Obesity

According to WHO, a body mass index (BMI) over 30 kg/m² in an adult is considered obesity.

Factors Which May Lead to Obesity

Obesity develops from a combination of factors. Obesity results from inheritance, environment, diet and lack of exercise combined. When energy intake remains greater than energy expenditure for a long time, fat accumulates and obesity results.

  • Genetic inheritance: can make a person prone to storing fat.
  • Environment: an environment with abundant energy-rich food and little physical work encourages weight gain.
  • Diet: eating excess fats and sugars, and overeating, are major causes.
  • Sedentary lifestyle: lack of exercise is a major cause.
  • Other factors: hormonal disorders and certain medications may also contribute.

Health Risks Involved in Obesity

Obesity increases the risk of many serious diseases. It is linked with type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, heart and cardiovascular diseases, stroke and certain cancers. Excess weight also strains joints, causing arthritis, and can disturb breathing during sleep. Long-term proper diet and regular physical activity are needed to control it.

Anorexia Nervosa

Anorexia nervosa is a psychological eating disorder in which a person has an intense fear of gaining weight and refuses to eat adequately. It is most common in young girls and women. The victim loses appetite and weight falls well below normal; some patients also practise induced vomiting. It can cause severe weakness, hormonal disturbance and even death if untreated. Treatment needs psychological help, medical care and proper nutrition.

lessons.title: Circulation — Need and Types
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Circulation?

Circulation is the transport of materials within the body through the heart and blood vessels, and in many animals through a lymphatic system as well. Cells continuously require oxygen and nutrients for metabolism and produce wastes that must be removed.

Need in Higher Animals

Higher animals are large and multicellular, so simple diffusion cannot supply all cells quickly enough: cells lie far from the body surface and from the gut, the rate of metabolism is high, and diffusion alone is too slow. Circulation is essential for survival of every cell.

  • Transport: oxygen, nutrients, hormones and waste products rapidly to and from every cell through blood vessels.
  • Other roles: distributes hormones, maintains body temperature, keeps pH and fluid balance, and carries antibodies and white blood cells for defence.

Circulation only transports wastes to the excretory organs; actual removal/excretion is performed by the kidneys etc., not by circulation itself.

Open and Closed Circulation

In a closed system blood is confined to vessels and remains distinct from the interstitial fluid surrounding the cells.

Arthropods have an open system: blood is not always confined to vessels. The heart pumps it through short arteries into open spaces (sinuses) of the body cavity, where it directly bathes the internal organs. There is no distinction between blood and interstitial fluid, so the general body fluid is called haemolymph. Blood returns slowly to the heart through small openings called ostia.

Single and Double Circuit Circulation

Single CircuitDouble Circuit
Heart passageOnce in one complete circuit; heart two-chambered, as in fishesTwice — pulmonary circuit to lungs and systemic circuit to body, as in amphibians to mammals
EfficiencyLess efficient oxygen supply to tissuesOxygenated and deoxygenated blood largely separate in birds and mammals; more efficient

Pulmonary and Systemic Circulation

Pulmonary: deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it is oxygenated, returning through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. It serves gaseous exchange; oxygenated blood in a pulmonary vein drains first into the left atrium.

Systemic: oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aorta to all body tissues, returning deoxygenated through the vena cava to the right atrium. It supplies the whole body. Together they form double circulation.

lessons.title: The Human Heart — Structure, Working and ECG
lessons.notes_html:
Structure of the Human Heart

A somewhat conical, muscular organ enclosed in the pericardium. Four chambers: two upper thin-walled atria and two lower thick-walled ventricles. Right and left sides are separated by inter-atrial and inter-ventricular septa, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix. Tricuspid and bicuspid valves guard the atrioventricular openings; semilunar valves guard the aorta and pulmonary artery. The wall is cardiac muscle (myocardium), covered externally and lined internally. The SA node in the right atrium acts as pacemaker.

SA Node — Pacemaker

It initiates each heartbeat, generating electrical impulses at a regular rhythm that spread over the atria, making them contract, and then reach the AV node and ventricles. It sets the normal rate and timing of pumping, about 70-75 times per minute at rest. Damage to the S.A node would disrupt the rate and timing of cardiac muscle contractions.

Flow of Blood Through the Heart

Body → vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → semilunar valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral) valve → left ventricle → semilunar valve → aorta → body.

When ventricles contract, the tricuspid and bicuspid valves close to prevent backflow and blood leaves through the semilunar valves, located where blood leaves via the aorta and pulmonary artery. Semilunar valves then close so blood cannot return to the ventricles. Valves thus ensure one-way flow.

Phases of Heartbeat

  • Atrial systole: both atria contract and push blood into the ventricles.
  • Ventricular systole: ventricles contract, atrioventricular valves close, blood is pumped into the aorta and pulmonary artery.
  • General diastole: the whole heart relaxes and fills with blood from the veins; the cycle repeats about 72 times per minute in a resting man.

LUB and DUB

LUB, the first, louder and longer sound, is produced when the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves close at the start of ventricular contraction. DUB, the second, shorter and sharper sound, is produced when the semilunar valves close at the end of ventricular contraction. Heard with a stethoscope, these sounds indicate proper working of the heart valves.

Electrocardiogram (ECG)

The graphical record of the electrical activity of the heart during a cardiac cycle, measured by electrodes placed on the body; it records impulses originating from the SA node and spreading through the heart muscle.

  • P wave: atrial depolarization and contraction.
  • QRS complex: ventricular depolarization.
  • T wave: ventricular repolarization and relaxation.

The shape and intervals of these waves show rate, rhythm and conduction of impulses from the SA node; any abnormality helps diagnose heart disorders.

lessons.title: Blood Vessels
lessons.notes_html:
Types of Blood Vessels in Man

Human blood vessels are of three types: arteries, veins and capillaries. Each vessel type is structurally suited to its function in circulation.

VesselStructureFunction
ArteriesThick, muscular and elastic walls with a narrow lumenCarry blood away from the heart under high pressure
VeinsThinner walls, a wider lumen and valves to prevent backflowCarry blood towards the heart under low pressure
CapillariesWall of only one layer of endothelium, connecting arterioles and venulesExchange of materials between blood and tissues

Capillaries and Exchange

Capillaries have walls of a single layer of endothelium so that exchange of materials can occur easily and rapidly. Oxygen, nutrients, hormones and waste products diffuse across this very thin wall between blood and tissue cells. A thicker wall would slow down this exchange. The huge number and total surface area of capillaries further increase the efficiency of exchange in the tissues.

Why Blood Flows Faster in Arteries

Blood flows faster in arteries because they receive blood directly from the pumping heart under high pressure. Arteries have narrower lumen relative to veins and thick elastic muscular walls that maintain this pressure. The total cross-sectional area of arteries is much less than that of capillaries, so velocity stays high. As blood reaches the wide capillary network and then veins, its speed and pressure decrease considerably.

lessons.title: Blood Pressure and Cardiovascular Disorders
lessons.notes_html:
Blood Pressure in the Vessels

Arteries receive blood directly from the pumping heart under high pressure, and their thick elastic muscular walls maintain this pressure. Blood pressure falls continuously as blood travels away from the heart. As blood reaches the wide capillary network and then veins, its speed and pressure decrease considerably.

  • Lowest pressure: Average blood pressure is lowest in the vena cava returning blood to the heart.
  • Pressure gradient: Pressure is higher in the vessels nearer the heart, such as the aorta and arteries, and falls through arterioles and capillaries towards the vena cava.

Vasoconstriction

Vasoconstriction is the narrowing of the blood vessels. Stress and certain hormones (e.g. adrenaline) cause vasoconstriction, narrowing the blood vessels. Stress or hormone concentration is therefore a cause of vasoconstriction.

Blood Clotting at a Damaged Surface

Clotting is initiated when platelets and plasma factors come in contact with an irregular (damaged/injured) surface. Contact with an irregular surface by platelets and other factors in plasma is the event that initiates blood clotting.

Disorders and Detection

The shape and intervals of the ECG waves show the rate, rhythm and conduction of impulses from the SA node, and any abnormality in the ECG helps diagnose heart disorders. Damage to the SA node would disrupt the rate and timing of cardiac muscle contractions, showing why normal conduction is essential for a regular heartbeat. The heart sounds LUB and DUB indicate the proper working of the heart valves, so their study also reflects the working of the valves during ventricular contraction.

lessons.title: Lymphatic System of Man
lessons.notes_html:
Lymph and Its Relation to Tissue Fluid

Lymph is essentially interstitial (tissue) fluid collected into lymph vessels, so it most closely resembles interstitial fluid. Lymph capillaries collect excess interstitial fluid from tissues and form lymph.

Parts of the Lymphatic System

The lymphatic system of man consists of lymph capillaries, lymph vessels, lymph nodes and lymphoid tissues such as the spleen.

  • Lymph capillaries: Collect excess interstitial fluid and absorbed fats from tissues; in villi they are called lacteals.
  • Lymph vessels: Lymph flows through larger vessels, which have one-way valves and are squeezed by nearby muscle contractions.
  • Lymph nodes: Lymph passes through lymph nodes where it is filtered and lymphocytes are produced.
  • Lymphoid tissues: Include tissues such as the spleen.

Return of Lymph to Blood

Finally lymph returns to the blood through the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct. The one-way valves in the lymph vessels and squeezing by nearby muscle contractions help lymph flow in one direction towards the blood.

Functions of the Lymphatic System

  • Fluid balance: It maintains fluid balance by collecting excess interstitial fluid from tissues and returning it to the blood.
  • Fat absorption: Lymph capillaries collect absorbed fats from tissues, and lacteals in the villi are involved in this collection.
  • Defence: This system defends the body; lymph is filtered in lymph nodes and lymphocytes are produced there.

Together, the collection of interstitial fluid, its filtration through lymph nodes, and its return through the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct keep tissue fluid balanced while supporting defence.

lessons.notes_html:
Immunology and the Lines of Defense

The study of the functioning and disorders of the immune system is termed immunology. The body is defended in successive lines. The first line of defense prevents pathogens from entering the body and acts non-specifically against any pathogen trying to enter.

Physical Barriers

The skin and mucous membrane serve as physical barriers in the first line of defense. The digestive tract has both kinds of barriers: physical barriers in the form of its mucous lining, and biochemical barriers such as HCl, enzymes and saliva.

Biochemical Barriers

Chemical defences form part of the first line of defense. Six biochemical barriers of the body are:

  • Hydrochloric acid (HCl): present in the stomach, it kills germs.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears and saliva that dissolves bacterial walls.
  • Acidic secretions: secretions of the skin and sweat check microbial growth.
  • Bile and digestive enzymes: they destroy many pathogens entering with food.
  • Mucus: it traps microbes.
  • Interferons and other antimicrobial proteins: they inhibit viruses and bacteria.

Together, the physical and biochemical barriers stop most pathogens at the body surfaces before they can cause infection.

lessons.title: Second Line of Defense — Inflammation, Phagocytosis and Fever
lessons.notes_html:
Ways of the Second Line of Defense

The second line of defense acts when pathogens cross the first line. These defences are non-specific but act rapidly:

  • Phagocytosis: by neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages and dendritic cells.
  • Natural killer cells: killing using perforin and granzymes.
  • Inflammation: brings more blood and phagocytes to the infected area.
  • Fever: inhibits microbial growth and speeds up defence reactions.
  • Antimicrobial proteins and complement: they also attack invading microbes.

Phagocytosis

Phagocytosis is the process by which certain white blood cells engulf and digest pathogens and dead material. The phagocyte extends pseudopodia around the microbe, encloses it in a vacuole, and lysosomal enzymes kill and digest it. Both neutrophils and macrophages are phagocytes that engulf and destroy bacteria. The main WBCs acting as phagocytes are neutrophils, monocytes (which become macrophages in tissues) and dendritic cells. Eosinophils also show limited phagocytic action.

Inflammation

Inflammation is the local protective response of tissues to infection or injury, marked by redness, heat, swelling and pain. It develops because damaged cells, mast cells and basophils release histamine and other mediators that dilate blood vessels and increase their permeability, so plasma and phagocytes accumulate at the site. Phagocytes destroy the pathogens and clean the debris, helping healing; thus inflammation limits infection and starts tissue repair. It is controlled by anti-inflammatory mechanisms: once the pathogen is removed, mediator release stops, antihistamines and steroids can reduce excessive response, and macrophages clean the area. Controlled inflammation is protective, but excessive inflammation can damage tissues.

Fever — Mechanism and Protective Role

Fever develops when pyrogens released by pathogens and immune cells act on the temperature centre (hypothalamus) and raise its set-point. The body then produces and conserves more heat by shivering and vasoconstriction until the new temperature is reached. Protectively, raised temperature inhibits the growth of many bacteria and viruses and speeds up phagocytosis and immune reactions. Mild fever itself is protective.

Harmful Effects of Fever and Antipyretic Therapy

High and prolonged fever increases metabolic rate and water loss, causing dehydration, weakness and discomfort. Very high temperature can denature enzymes and damage tissues, especially of the brain. In children, sudden high fever may cause convulsions (fits). Prolonged fever also reduces appetite and can disturb heart and kidney function, so it must be controlled. Antipyretic therapy is the use of medicines that lower body temperature during fever, e.g. paracetamol. It is used when fever becomes very high or prolonged, because excessive fever can damage body proteins, cause discomfort, dehydration and convulsions, especially in children. By reducing the raised set-point of temperature in the hypothalamus, antipyretics bring relief, and are used mainly to control harmful effects of high fever.

lessons.title: Third Line of Defense — Antibodies and Cell-Mediated Immunity
lessons.notes_html:
The Specific Immune Response

The third line of defense, consisting of T and B lymphocytes and antibodies, is responsible for the specific immune response. Any foreign substance that can elicit an immune response is called an antigen.

How a Bacterium Is Identified as Non-Self

A bacterium is identified as non-self because its surface carries antigens and molecular patterns different from the body's own markers. Antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells engulf the bacterium and display its antigen fragments on their surface with MHC-II molecules. Helper T cells recognize this antigen-MHC combination as foreign, because body cells display only self antigens with MHC. This recognition activates the specific immune response. Self cells are protected because lymphocytes that react against self antigens are normally eliminated or inactivated. All nucleated cells exhibit MHC-I receptors, while MHC-II is found on specialized antigen-presenting cells like macrophages. Neutrophils are phagocytic but are not involved in antigen presentation.

Antibodies — Structure, Secretion and Differences

Antibodies are secreted by plasma cells, which are activated B cells transformed into antibody-producing cells. An antibody is a Y-shaped protein made of four polypeptide chains: two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains, joined by disulfide bonds. The stem and lower parts form constant regions, while the tips of the arms have variable regions that form two identical antigen-binding sites, specific for one antigen.

Even though the core proteins are the same, antibodies differ in their variable regions. The variable regions have different amino acid sequences, forming antigen-binding sites of different shapes, so each antibody binds a specific antigen. Antibodies also differ in their class (type of heavy chain), which determines their function and location, e.g. in blood, secretions or on mast cells.

How Antibodies Get Rid of Pathogens

Antibodies bind antigens, neutralizing toxins and viruses, clumping (agglutinating) microbes, and marking them for phagocytosis (opsonization). They also activate complement, which lyses the pathogen.

Natural Passive Immunity

Transfer of ready-made antibodies from mother to her fetus is natural passive immunity, as the fetus's own immune system does not produce them.

Cytotoxicity — NK Cell and Tc Cell

Cytotoxicity is the killing of target cells (infected or tumor cells) by immune cells through toxic substances. Both NK cells and Tc cells kill by releasing perforin, which makes pores in the target cell membrane, and granzymes, which enter through these pores and induce the target cell to die.

FeatureNK CellTc Cell
DefenseInnate, non-specific, second lineSpecific, third line, adaptive immunity
ActivationWithout prior sensitization and without antigen presentation; acts immediatelyActivated by specific antigens presented with MHC-I
MemoryNot antigen-specific, no memoryAntigen-specific, forms memory cells
KillingPerforin and granzymesPerforin and granzymes

The main difference is specificity and the need for activation: Tc cells are antigen-specific and have memory, NK cells are not.

How Tumour Cells Are Dealt With

The immune system constantly surveys the body for abnormal cells, including tumor cells, which display altered antigens on their surface. NK cells and cytotoxic T cells (Tc) recognize these abnormal cells as non-self and kill them by cytotoxicity, using perforin and granzymes. Macrophages also engulf dead tumor cells. This immune surveillance prevents many tumors from developing.

lessons.notes_html:
Autoimmune Disorders

An autoimmune disorder is an abnormality in which the immune system fails to recognize one or more of its own tissues as self and attacks them, producing self-antibodies that destroy own cells. In all these disorders, the immune system fails to recognize its own tissues as self, and misdirected self-antibodies destroy the body's own cells.

Four Autoimmune Disorders of Man

  • Type-I diabetes mellitus: immune cells destroy insulin-producing cells of the pancreas.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: joints are attacked causing pain and deformity.
  • Psoriasis: a skin disorder with rapid abnormal skin growth.
  • Multiple sclerosis / myasthenia-type disorders: nervous or muscle tissues are attacked.

Type-I diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis are also given as examples of autoimmune disorders in which self-antibodies destroy own cells.

Transplant Rejection — Role of T Cells and B Cells

In transplant rejection, the recipient's helper T cells recognize the donor organ as foreign through antigen-presenting cells, proliferate, and activate NK cells and cytotoxic T cells that directly attack the grafted tissue. This is cell-mediated rejection.

The activated helper T cells also signal B cells to become plasma cells whose antibodies destroy the graft. This is humoral rejection.

For this reason transplant patients are given immunosuppressant drugs.

lessons.title: Respiration and the Human Respiratory System
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Respiration?

Respiration is the process of exchanging gases with the environment and releasing energy from food; breathing is its mechanical part, consisting of inhalation and exhalation. The exchange of gases between the external environment and the lungs (blood at alveoli) is called external respiration.

How Breathing Developed in Animals

Breathing developed when animals became large and multicellular and simple diffusion through the body surface was no longer sufficient. Aquatic animals first developed gills for extracting oxygen from water. With the invasion of land, lungs and tracheal systems evolved to take oxygen directly from air, step by step with increasing body size, activity and terrestrial life.

Parts of the Human Respiratory System

The system comprises the nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and lungs containing millions of alveoli, where oxygen diffuses into blood and CO2 diffuses out. The diaphragm, ribs and intercostal muscles bring about breathing movements, and the lungs are protected by pleural membranes. The trachea, supported by C-shaped cartilage rings, divides into two primary bronchi, one entering each lung, branching into smaller bronchi and bronchioles ending in alveoli. The right lung has three lobes, the left lung two lobes, and below the lungs lies the dome-shaped diaphragm.

Passage of Air to the Alveoli

External nares → nasal cavity → internal nares → pharynx → larynx → trachea → primary bronchi → secondary bronchi → tertiary bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveoli. Air enters through the mouth and nose and travels via the windpipe (trachea) to the lungs, filtered, warmed and moistened in the nasal cavity and trachea on its way.

Key Structures

  • Alveoli: The tiny air sacs in human lungs; gaseous exchange takes place here, their thin moist walls surrounded by blood capillaries.
  • Nasal chambers: Function as an air conditioner, warming, moistening and filtering incoming air.
  • Larynx: A cartilage organ connecting pharynx to trachea; it houses the vocal cords and its epiglottis guards the trachea.
  • Trachea: Conducts air and filters it through mucus and cilia, which trap dust and germs.

Three Regions of the Pharynx

The pharynx is a common passage for air and food.

  • Nasopharynx: Behind the nasal cavity; only passes air; openings of the auditory (Eustachian) tubes equalize air pressure.
  • Oropharynx: Behind the oral cavity; passes both air and food; contains the tonsils that help in defence.
  • Laryngopharynx: Lowest part, leading to the larynx for air and the oesophagus for food; the epiglottis directs food away from the windpipe during swallowing.

Five Main Functions

  • Gaseous exchange: Taking in oxygen and removing carbon dioxide.
  • Oxygen supply: Supplying oxygen for cellular respiration and energy production.
  • Blood pH regulation: Helping regulate blood pH by controlling CO2 level.
  • Sound production: Through the vocal cords in the larynx.
  • Protection and smell: Filtering, warming and moistening air, trapping germs in mucus, and sense of smell in the nasal cavity.

These functions keep the internal environment stable.

lessons.title: Mechanism of Breathing
lessons.notes_html:
Type of Ventilation in Humans

Humans show pulmonary ventilation by negative pressure breathing (also described as tidal ventilation). Air is drawn into the lungs by expanding the chest cavity with the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, and the same pathway is used for air leaving the lungs. The same air passage therefore works in both directions, and fresh air mixes with some residual air in the lungs. Ventilation rate in a healthy adult is about 15-18 breaths per minute at rest.

Why It Is Called Negative Pressure Breathing

Human breathing is called negative pressure breathing because air is sucked into the lungs by creating a pressure inside the lungs lower than atmospheric pressure. When the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the rib cage expands, the volume of the chest cavity increases and pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure. Air therefore rushes in from outside to equalize the pressure. During expiration the process reverses and air is pushed out.

Inspiration and Expiration

FeatureInspirationExpiration
Type of processActive processNormally passive
Diaphragm and musclesDiaphragm contracts and flattens; external intercostal muscles lift the ribs up and outDiaphragm and intercostal muscles relax
Chest cavity volumeIncreasesDecreases
Pressure in lungsFalls below atmospheric pressureIncreased pressure in the lungs
Movement of airAir rushes in through the air passage to the alveoliAir is pushed out of the lungs

One complete inspiration and expiration forms one breath cycle.

Control of Breathing

Involuntary breathing is controlled by neurons located in the respiratory centres of the medulla and pons.

Why the Rate of Breathing Increases

The rate of breathing increases when the body needs more oxygen and produces more carbon dioxide, e.g. during exercise, exertion, fever or stress. Increased CO2 and H+ concentration in the blood is detected by chemoreceptors in the aortic and carotid bodies. They send signals to the respiratory centre in the medulla, which increases the rate and depth of breathing. This removes extra CO2 and restores normal blood pH and oxygen supply.

Total Lung Capacity

The maximum volume of air contained in the lungs after a full forced inhalation is the total lung capacity.

lessons.title: Exchange and Transport of Gases
lessons.notes_html:
Exchange of Gases at the Alveolar Level

At the alveolar level, exchange occurs by simple diffusion across the very thin (about 1 micrometre) barrier between alveolar air and blood capillaries. Oxygen concentration is higher in alveoli than in the incoming blood, so oxygen diffuses into the blood and binds with haemoglobin. Carbon dioxide concentration is higher in blood than in alveoli, so it diffuses out into the alveoli and is exhaled. The large surface area, moist surface and rich capillary network make this exchange very rapid and efficient. Gaseous exchange takes place in the alveoli, whose thin moist walls are surrounded by blood capillaries.

Haemoglobin — The Respiratory Pigment

Haemoglobin is called the respiratory pigment in humans and many animals. It is a red, iron-containing protein present in red blood cells. Each haemoglobin molecule can carry up to four oxygen molecules, forming oxyhaemoglobin, and transports oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. About 97% of oxygen in the body is transported by haemoglobin, while only about 3% is carried dissolved in plasma.

How CO2 Is Transported from Cells to the Lungs

Carbon dioxide produced in cells diffuses into blood capillaries and is transported to the lungs. Blood carries it through veins to the heart and then through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. At the alveoli, CO2 is released and exhaled.

Way of CO2 transportShareHow it is carried
Dissolved in plasmaAbout 5-7%A small part dissolves in the blood plasma
As carbaminohaemoglobinAbout 20-23%Binds with haemoglobin in red blood cells to form carbaminohaemoglobin
As bicarbonate ionsMajor part, about 70%Converted in RBCs, with the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, into carbonic acid which dissociates into bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) and H+; bicarbonate is carried in plasma as KHCO3 and NaHCO3

At the lungs these reactions are reversed and CO2 is released for exhalation.

lessons.title: Respiratory Disorders
lessons.notes_html:
Protection of the Air Passages

This chapter does not describe named respiratory diseases in detail. Its disorder-related content is about how the air passages are protected from dust, germs and infection, and how the entry of food and pathogens into the windpipe is prevented. When these defences work, the respiratory surface stays clean and the lungs are protected from infection and damage.

Hair, Mucus and Cilia

  • Hair in the nostrils: Traps large dust particles and prevents them from entering the air passages.
  • Mucus glands: Mucus glands in the nostrils and trachea secrete sticky mucus that traps fine dust, pollen and germs carried by inhaled air.
  • Cilia: Cilia on the lining then sweep the mucus with trapped particles towards the pharynx, from where it is swallowed or expelled.
  • Trachea: The trachea filters the air we breathe through its mucus and cilia, which trap dust and germs.
  • Nasal chambers: The nasal chambers warm, moisten and filter the incoming air, functioning as an air conditioner.

Together, hair and mucus keep the respiratory surface clean and protect the lungs from infection and damage. Protection of air passages by filtering, warming and moistening air and trapping germs in mucus is one of the main functions of the respiratory system.

Guards Against Entry into the Windpipe

  • Epiglottis: The epiglottis of the larynx guards the trachea, and in the laryngopharynx it directs food away from the windpipe during swallowing, leading air to the larynx and food to the oesophagus.
  • Tonsils: The oropharynx contains the tonsils that help in defence.
  • Pleural membranes: The lungs are protected by pleural membranes.

Breathing Change in Fever

The rate of breathing increases when the body needs more oxygen and produces more carbon dioxide, e.g. during exercise, exertion, fever or stress. Increased CO2 and H+ concentration in the blood is detected by chemoreceptors, which signal the respiratory centre in the medulla to increase the rate and depth of breathing, removing extra CO2 and restoring normal blood pH and oxygen supply.
